textRun.content: System Design Interview — How to Approach It

a step-by-step approach, functional vs non-functional requirements, back-of-the-envelope estimation, a reusable master template, communication, deep dives, trade-offs, common mistakes, and a worked example.
1. What is a System Design Interview?

A system design interview is an open-ended technical discussion in which you design a software system under a set of functional, scale, reliability, and business constraints. There is rarely one correct architecture. Interviewers evaluate how you turn ambiguity into a structured design and how you defend trade-offs.
The interview evaluates your reasoning process as much as the final architecture.
You usually receive a broad prompt such as 'Design a URL shortener', 'Design Twitter', or 'Design a payment system'.
The interviewer intentionally leaves details unspecified so you must ask questions and make assumptions.
You are expected to move from requirements to a high-level design and then deep-dive into important components.
The interviewer may change requirements mid-discussion to see whether your architecture and reasoning adapt.
Asks targeted questions and defines scope
Breaks problem into understandable services/data flows
One giant box or chaotic component list
Explains why option A fits better than B
Says one technology is always best
Assumes every dependency is always available
Spends equal time on every minor feature
Expectations vary by company and level, but a useful mental model is:
Understand common building blocks and basic scaling
Clear requirements, APIs, DB, cache, LB, simple failure handling
Make sensible trade-offs and identify bottlenecks
Partitioning, consistency, async processing, HA, capacity reasoning
Drive ambiguous design, operational concerns, migration and org trade-offs
Multi-region, SLOs, failure domains, cost, evolution, risk
A practical time budget for a roughly 45-minute design discussion.
1.  Clarify the problem and define the must-have functional scope.
2.  Capture non-functional requirements and scale assumptions.
3.  Do quick back-of-the-envelope estimates if they change architecture choices.
4.  Define key APIs/events and the main data model/access patterns.
5.  Draw the high-level architecture and explain the main request flows.
6.  Identify bottlenecks and deep-dive into the most important component(s).
7.  Address scalability, reliability, consistency, security, observability, and cost where relevant.
8.  Summarize trade-offs, known limitations, and what you would improve next.
The first few questions should reduce ambiguity, not demonstrate trivia.
What features are explicitly out of scope?
Is this read-heavy, write-heavy, or balanced?
Are objects small metadata records, large files, streams, or messages?
Does the interviewer care more about availability, consistency, latency, or cost?
Are we designing globally or for one region?
Before I design, I want to clarify the main user flows and scale so I optimize for the right thing.
Core experience required for system to be meaningful
Clarify features first, then quality targets, then measurable assumptions.
Functional requirements describe what users and systems must be able to do.
Phrase requirements as actions: 'User can upload a photo', 'User can request a shortened URL'.
Prioritize primary flows over administrative or edge functionality.
Identify reads and writes because they later drive APIs, schema, caches, and partitions.
Include system-to-system flows when they matter, e.g. asynchronous notification delivery.
If you can express it as an operation or workflow the system must perform, it is usually functional.
NFRs define the quality bar and constraints that shape the architecture.
Must every read see latest write?
Instead of 'low latency', use a target such as p95 < 200 ms for an interactive API.
Instead of 'highly available', clarify whether 99.9%, 99.99%, or disaster recovery is expected.
Instead of 'large scale', estimate DAU, peak QPS, data size, and growth.
Instead of 'consistent', identify which operations require read-after-write or strong ordering.
Do not invent precise requirements if the interviewer has not provided them. State reasonable assumptions and ask for agreement.

Back-of-the-envelope estimation uses rough arithmetic to determine the order of magnitude of traffic, storage, bandwidth, or memory. Its purpose is to influence design choices, not to predict production bills exactly.
Estimates connect product assumptions to architecture decisions.
Use round numbers so arithmetic remains easy.
Estimate only dimensions that matter to the design.
Sanity-check the final number; exact precision is unnecessary.
Use a peak multiplier because real traffic is not uniformly distributed.
Requests/day ÷ 100,000 gives an easy approximate average QPS.
Keep a small formula sheet in memory; derive everything else from assumptions.
Peak QPS = average QPS × peak multiplier (often 2-10× depending on workload).
Cache working set ≈ number of hot objects × average object size.
Streaming: Focus on throughput and bandwidth.
Blob Storage: Focus on object size, upload/download bandwidth, and storage.
Chat: Focus on concurrent connections and message fan-out.
Rule: Estimate only what impacts design decisions.
Good estimation is selective. Spending 10 minutes calculating numbers that never affect the architecture wastes interview time.
Defining the main interfaces helps make request flows concrete.
Mention key request/response fields, not every HTTP header.
Use APIs to expose access patterns that the data model must support.
Write the key fields used by the main access patterns.
Choose identifiers and primary lookup keys.
Identify high-volume indexes or secondary access patterns.
Only then choose SQL/NoSQL/storage technology based on requirements.
Access patterns should influence the data model. Do not begin with 'I will use MongoDB/Postgres' and force the schema to fit later.
Draw the smallest architecture that can support the core requirements. Explain the main request path end to end.
Search/indexing or analytics only when the requirements need them.
Start with the whole system, then zoom in on the highest-value deep dive.
18. Explain Data Flow, Not Just Boxes
For every important flow, narrate what happens:
Read checks cache or storage; write persists durable state.
Async side-effects are published to queue/stream if needed.
Response is returned; caches/indexes may be updated.
Weak: 'I have Redis, Kafka, Cassandra.' Strong: 'Reads check Redis by URL code; on a miss the service reads the sharded mapping store, then caches the mapping with a TTL.'
19. Step 6 — Identify the Bottleneck / Deep Dive
Which operation has the highest QPS?
Which path has the tightest latency?
Which component is a single point of failure?
Which operation needs the strongest consistency?
Where will fan-out or hot keys occur?
Partitioning strategy, feed generation, cache consistency, unique ID generation, message delivery, search indexing, multi-region failover, rate limiting, or exactly-once-like payment behavior.
High Availability: Multiple instances across availability zones.
Retries: Timeouts, limited retries, and backoff.
Dead-Letter Queue: Handle repeatedly failed jobs.
Monitoring: Track SLOs and set alerts.
What happens if this dependency is slow, unavailable, duplicated, or returns a partial response?
Do users need to read their own writes immediately?
What is the source of truth?
For money/inventory/unique usernames, stronger correctness guarantees may matter more than raw availability.
Instead of 'eventual consistency is fine', say exactly WHICH reads may be stale, for HOW LONG, and WHY the product can tolerate it.
TLS in transit and encryption at rest.
Sensitive-data minimization, retention, audit, and deletion.
Mention security early enough to show awareness, but do not let generic security boilerplate consume the design unless security is central to the prompt.
Request rate, error rate, latency, saturation.
Business KPIs such as successful orders/messages delivered.
Alerts tied to actionable user impact.
Use this as your reusable interview backbone.
Functional scope, out of scope, actors, use cases
Core interfaces, entities, keys, access patterns
Hardest path, data partitioning, cache, async workflow
Alternatives, limitations, security, observability, next steps
27. How to Communicate During the Interview
Think aloud, but keep your explanation structured.
Ask short alignment questions after major steps.
Use the diagram as a shared map, not as decoration.
Explain the WHY behind important components.
If the interviewer challenges a choice, treat it as collaboration rather than defense.
If stuck, identify the requirement that matters most and compare two options.

I see two reasonable options. If low write latency matters most, I prefer A. If immediate global consistency matters most, I would accept the extra latency of B. Which direction should we optimize for?
28. Things to Avoid During a System Design Interview
Most weak interviews fail because of process and communication, not lack of exotic technology.
You may solve the wrong problem or overbuild.
Small requirement changes can invalidate the memorized answer.
Tools are not explanations; describe why each component exists.
Do not spend 15 minutes on ID generation before drawing the overall system.
Scale, latency, availability, durability, and consistency drive the architecture.
You cannot justify scale mechanisms without knowing the rough scale.
Do not add Kafka, microservices, multi-region, and sharding without a requirement.
Every meaningful design choice has downsides.
The interviewer cannot evaluate reasoning you do not communicate.
When data is missing, state a reasonable assumption and continue.
Interviewer hints often indicate the area they want you to explore.
29. Mini Worked Example — Design a URL Shortener
A simple first architecture before discussing deeper scaling choices.
Create a short URL from a long URL.
Redirect short code to original URL.
Read-heavy; redirects should be low latency and highly available.
~100M redirects/day -> ~1K average read QPS, perhaps ~5K peak in our assumption.
~1.8 TB/year of mapping metadata at our rough 500-byte assumption.
Mapping table: shortCode -> longURL, createdAt, expiry, ownerId
Stateless API service behind load balancer.
Optional async analytics pipeline so redirect latency is not blocked by counters.
How are unique short codes generated?
How do we shard mappings if data grows?
How do we prevent malicious links/abuse?
What consistency is needed after a URL is created?
30. Interviewer Follow-Up Questions You Should Expect
What is the bottleneck in your current design?
What happens if the database is down?
What happens if one region goes down?
How would this change at 100× traffic?
How do you handle a hot key or celebrity user?
What happens when a message/job is processed twice?
How do you partition the data?
How would you monitor this system?
How would you migrate from the simple design to the scaled design?
Did I clarify 3-5 core requirements and scope?
Can someone understand main flow in 60 seconds?
Did I connect schema/keys to access patterns?
Did I spend time on one meaningful hard area?
Did I explain at least 2 meaningful trade-offs?
Did I narrate and check alignment?
Who uses it? Core flows? In/out of scope?
Scale, latency, availability, durability, consistency, security
Average/peak QPS, storage, bandwidth only where useful
Cache, replicate, partition, async, CDN as justified
System Design Basics — Detailed Glossary & Building Blocks
These components recur across almost every real system design problem.
System design is the process of defining the major components, data stores, interfaces, data flows, and reliability/scaling mechanisms needed to satisfy product requirements.
: DNS, CDN, reverse proxy, API gateway, load balancer.
: stateless APIs, stateful services, workers, functions.
: SQL/NoSQL DB, cache, object storage, search index.
: queues, streams, event buses, background jobs.
Distributed systems must balance multiple measurable properties.
Ability to handle more users, traffic, data, or geographic scope.
Vertical scaling adds resources to a node; horizontal scaling adds nodes/partitions.
Probability that the service can respond successfully when requested.
System consistently produces correct outcomes over time.
A system can be available but unreliable if it returns wrong/corrupt results.
Ability to continue despite component failures.
Requires redundancy, failure detection, isolation, retry/failover strategy.
Latency, throughput, bandwidth, queueing, and tail behavior.
Observability, deployability, operability, capacity planning, debugging.
A load balancer distributes requests and removes unhealthy targets from normal service.
Prevents one server from becoming the only entry point or bottleneck.
Allows horizontal scaling behind one stable endpoint.
Supports health checks and failure removal.
May terminate TLS and perform L7 host/path/header routing.
Can be Layer 4 (connections) or Layer 7 (HTTP-aware requests).
The load balancer itself must be redundant; otherwise it becomes a SPOF.
Cloud-managed LBs generally hide this redundancy; self-managed proxies need multiple instances and failover.
Stateless backends allow any request to go to any healthy instance.
Sticky sessions simplify local session state but can cause uneven load and difficult failover.
I use load balancing when I need multiple interchangeable service instances. It gives scale-out and health-aware failover, but the backend should ideally be stateless so routing remains flexible.
Algorithm choice depends on request cost, connection duration, node capacity, and affinity needs.
Pick two random servers and send to the less loaded one. This often achieves strong balance with much less global coordination than finding the absolute least-loaded server.
Round robin is fine when requests are homogeneous. For long-lived or variable-cost connections, least-connections/latency-aware routing usually reflects backend pressure better.
Forward proxy hides/controls clients; reverse proxy hides/controls servers.
Client deliberately sends outbound traffic through proxy.
Common for corporate egress, privacy, filtering, caching, network policy.
Clients call the reverse proxy as if it were the application.
Routes to internal services, terminates TLS, caches, compresses, filters, authenticates.
Can implement retries/timeouts/rate limits, but careless retries can amplify outages.
Roles overlap. A reverse proxy may load-balance; a load balancer may implement reverse-proxy functions.
In interviews, describe the responsibility rather than arguing over product labels.
A proxy mediates communication. Forward proxy represents clients going out; reverse proxy represents servers receiving traffic and is often where routing, TLS, policy, and load balancing happen.
Caching can exist at several layers; each layer has different scope and freshness.
Primary benefits: lower latency, higher read throughput, reduced DB/API cost.
Main risks: stale data, invalidation bugs, cache stampede, hot keys, memory pressure.
Stampede: many requests miss one hot key simultaneously.
Penetration: repeated requests for nonexistent keys bypass cache.
Hot key: one key concentrates traffic on one cache node.
Eviction storm: memory pressure causes hit ratio collapse.
Stale cache: invalidation/update lag returns old data.
Cache read/write pattern decides who loads and who persists data.
Database choice follows data model and access patterns.
Flexible query language and mature tooling.
Strong fit for business invariants and evolving analytical queries.
Wide-column: large partitioned sparse datasets, write-heavy workloads.
NoSQL does not automatically mean eventual consistency.
SQL does not automatically mean single-node scale.
Discuss the exact database guarantees and access patterns.
I start from access patterns, transaction/consistency needs, data relationships, and scaling model. SQL and NoSQL are families, not binary quality levels.
Partitioning spreads storage and traffic across nodes.
High cardinality and even traffic distribution.
JOINs, transactions, aggregation, and sorting become more expensive.
Rebalancing data during node changes must be controlled.
Sharding solves one-node storage/write limits, but the partition key is a long-term architectural decision. I choose a key that distributes load and aligns with the dominant query.
Indexes reduce read work by maintaining an auxiliary search structure.
B/B+ tree indexes: equality + ordered range queries.
Hash indexes: equality lookup, not ordered range scanning.
Inverted indexes: full-text search maps terms to documents.
Covering index: query can be answered from index without fetching base row.
Every insert/update/delete may update several indexes.
Too many indexes can make write-heavy systems much slower.
Low-selectivity indexes may not help much.
I index the fields used in important filters, joins, sort/order, and lookups. I avoid blindly indexing every field because indexes add write amplification and storage.
Replication creates copies; redundancy also applies to services, networks, and whole failure domains.
Recent acknowledged writes may be at risk
Read replica may return older data.
Read-after-write UX may need primary/session-consistent reads.
Lag grows during write spikes or slow replicas.
Replication improves availability and read capacity, but I must specify sync/async behavior, failover rules, replica lag expectations, and how stale reads are handled.
CAP is specifically about behavior when network partition occurs.
Consistency (C): all clients see a single up-to-date value according to the model.
Availability (A): every request to a nonfailed node receives a response.
Partition tolerance (P): system continues despite dropped/delayed communication between groups of nodes.
In a real distributed system, network partitions must be tolerated.
During a partition, the system must choose whether to preserve strong consistency or continue serving potentially divergent operations.
CP system may reject/block some requests.
AP system may serve stale/conflicting data and reconcile later.
CAP does not mean 'choose any two all the time'. The hard trade-off becomes unavoidable specifically during a partition.
For an inventory reservation I may choose consistency during partition and reject some writes. For a social feed, availability with temporary divergence can be acceptable.
PACELC extends CAP to normal operation.
If there is a Partition (P), do we choose Availability (A) or Consistency (C)?
Else (E), during normal operation, do we optimize Latency (L) or Consistency (C)?
Most of the system's lifetime is not during a partition.
Strong cross-region consistency can add coordination latency every day.
A database may be CP under partition but still choose lower latency/eventual reads normally, or vice versa.
CAP tells me what happens during a partition; PACELC makes me also discuss the normal-day latency-versus-consistency cost of coordination.
Consistent hashing minimizes remapping when the cluster membership changes.
Hash nodes and keys into the same logical ring.
A key is assigned to the next node clockwise (one common model).
Adding/removing a node changes only nearby key ranges rather than most keys.
Each physical node owns many positions on the ring.
Lets high-capacity machines own more virtual positions.
Consistent hashing is useful when nodes frequently join/leave and I want minimal key movement. Virtual nodes improve balance and capacity weighting.
Quorum uses overlapping read/write replica sets.
W = number of replicas that must acknowledge a write.
A classic overlap condition is R + W > N, so a read set intersects the latest write set.
W=2, R=2: stronger overlap but both reads and writes require multiple replicas.
W=1, R=3: low write latency but expensive reads.
W=3, R=1: strong write coordination but quick reads.
Overlap alone does not magically guarantee linearizability; versioning, conflict resolution, concurrent writes, clocks, and database protocol matter.
I use quorum language to describe how many replicas participate in reads and writes. Higher R/W coordination can improve freshness/durability but costs latency and availability.
A leader serializes decisions/writes; followers replicate and may serve reads.
Leader handles writes or consensus decisions.
Followers may serve read traffic if stale reads are acceptable.
When leader fails, healthy nodes need a new leader.
Election requires coordination/consensus to avoid two leaders making conflicting decisions.
Old leader returning after isolation must not act as current leader.
Two nodes both believe they are leader.
Use consensus terms/epochs/fencing tokens to prevent stale leader actions.
Leader/follower simplifies write ordering. The difficult parts are failure detection, election, fencing the old leader, replica catch-up, and deciding whether follower reads may be stale.
Heartbeats provide failure suspicion, not perfect knowledge.
After a timeout, node is suspected failed and failover/election may begin.
Network congestion can delay heartbeat even when node is healthy.
Stop-the-world GC or CPU pause can mimic failure.
Timeout too small = false failovers; too large = slow recovery.
More advanced systems estimate failure suspicion statistically rather than using one hard timeout.
A missing heartbeat is evidence, not proof, of failure. I choose timeout based on network/runtime behavior and design the system to tolerate false suspicion safely.
Checksums detect accidental corruption in storage and transfer.
Checksums often optimize fast accidental-error detection.
Cryptographic hashes also aim to resist intentional collision/preimage attacks.
Checksums are an integrity-detection mechanism. They tell me that bytes are corrupted; replication/parity/backups are what let me repair or recover.
Bloom filter saves expensive lookups by cheaply rejecting keys that are definitely absent.
Each inserted key is hashed by multiple hash functions; corresponding bits are set.
Lookup: if any required bit is zero -> key definitely not present.
If all bits are one -> key may be present.
Classic Bloom filter may say 'maybe present' for an absent item.
It does not say 'definitely absent' for an item that was inserted, assuming no unsupported deletion/corruption.
Avoid disk/SSTable lookup when key definitely absent.
Bloom filters trade a configurable false-positive rate for very small memory use. They are valuable when a negative lookup is expensive.
Real-time does not always mean WebSockets.
Make receiver idempotent because duplicate delivery is normal.
Use event IDs and delivery logs.

I choose the lightest real-time mechanism that fits direction and latency. WebSockets are for true bidirectional sessions; SSE is simpler one-way browser streaming; webhooks are server-to-server callbacks.
A scalable application often combines these concepts in one request path:
Durable source of truth and fast lookup
Scenario: One service instance cannot handle peak traffic.
Put stateless instances behind a load balancer and scale horizontally.
Add correct indexes first; then consider cache/read replicas if needed.
Scenario: One database node cannot hold/write all data.
Partition/shard by a carefully selected key.
Scenario: Adding cache nodes causes massive remapping.
Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.
Scenario: Need fast negative lookups before hitting disk.
Use a Bloom filter when false positives are acceptable.
Scenario: Need to know whether a worker is alive.
Use heartbeats/failure detection, while accounting for false positives.
Scenario: Need read scale but writes have one canonical order.
Scenario: Network partition occurs during inventory update.
Favor consistency/correctness and reject/block unsafe writes.
Scenario: Social feed replica is temporarily behind.
Eventual consistency may be acceptable if product semantics allow it.
Scenario: Chat needs bidirectional real-time communication.
Use WebSockets and design connection ownership/reconnect/backpressure.
Scenario: Payment provider must notify your backend.
Use signed webhooks with retries and idempotent processing.
Availability is ability to answer; reliability also concerns correct behavior over time.
CAP means choose any two forever
The C/A trade-off is forced during network partition.
Replicas can copy corruption/deletion; backups provide historical recovery.
Indexes speed selected reads but increase storage and write cost.
Usually cache is disposable acceleration; durable state belongs elsewhere.
It only says 'maybe present' or 'definitely absent'.
Timeout gives suspicion; network delay can cause false positives.
It minimizes movement; some keys still move.
WebSocket is best real-time protocol for everything
SSE, long polling, polling, push, or webhooks can be simpler.
Components run on multiple networked machines and coordinate to provide one logical service; partial failures and network uncertainty become fundamental concerns.
Availability measures whether service can respond; reliability measures whether it continues to behave correctly over time. A service can be available yet return incorrect results.
The ability to continue acceptable operation despite component failures, usually through redundancy, isolation, detection, and failover.
To distribute traffic across healthy instances, enable horizontal scaling, and remove unhealthy targets from normal routing.
Round robin ignores current workload and cycles evenly; least connections adapts to long-lived/uneven connections by favoring less-busy targets.
Forward proxy represents clients to external servers; reverse proxy represents backend servers to clients.
It lowers latency and reduces backend/database load by reusing previously fetched/computed results.
Many clients simultaneously miss an expired/hot key and all hit the backing store, potentially overloading it.
A disproportionately popular key that concentrates requests on one partition/cache node.
SQL is strong for relations, transactions, and flexible queries; NoSQL families often optimize known access patterns and distributed partitioning. Exact product guarantees matter.
Partitioning one logical dataset across multiple nodes so storage/write/read load is distributed.
12. What makes a good shard key?
High cardinality, even load, alignment with common queries, and low risk of hotspots/cross-shard operations.
13. What does a database index cost?
Extra storage and additional work on writes/updates/deletes; it speeds selected read patterns.
Replication keeps live copies for availability/read scale; backups keep recoverable historical copies and protect against logical corruption/deletion.
Sync waits for replica acknowledgement before success, improving durability/freshness at higher latency; async returns sooner but may expose lag/recent-data-loss risk.
During a network partition, a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee both strong consistency and full availability.
It also asks, when no partition exists, whether the design trades latency for consistency.
A partitioning method that minimizes key movement when nodes join/leave by mapping keys and nodes into a shared hash space/ring.
To improve distribution, smoother rebalancing, and capacity weighting in consistent-hash clusters.
A rule requiring a configured number of replicas for reads/writes; overlapping sets can improve freshness/consistency depending on the database protocol.
N is replica count, R is replicas consulted for a read, W is replicas acknowledging a write.
One leader orders/accepts writes and followers replicate its state; followers may serve reads based on consistency needs.
Multiple nodes simultaneously act as leader for the same authority, risking conflicting state.
A periodic liveness signal used for failure detection/suspicion.
25. Why can heartbeat detection be wrong?
Network delay, packet loss, runtime pauses, or CPU overload can hide a healthy node and cause false suspicion.
A compact value computed from data and later recomputed to detect accidental corruption.
27. Does a checksum repair corrupted data?
No. It detects mismatch; replication, parity, or backup is needed for recovery.
A probabilistic set structure that can say definitely absent or maybe present using very little memory.
29. Bloom filter false positive vs false negative?
Classic Bloom filters can return false positives but not false negatives for inserted items under their normal assumptions.
Before expensive storage/database lookups when many queries are for keys that do not exist.
Polling sends repeated requests at intervals; long polling keeps a request open until data arrives or timeout.
WebSocket is bidirectional; SSE is one-way server-to-browser streaming over HTTP and is simpler for server-driven updates.
WebSocket is a persistent interactive client/server channel; webhook is a server-to-server event callback.
34. Which concepts most often combine in a scalable read-heavy service?
Load balancing, caching, database indexing, read replication, partitioning if necessary, and observability/failure handling.
35. What is the best way to use glossary concepts in an interview?
Introduce them only when a requirement or bottleneck justifies them, then explain the benefit, failure mode, and trade-off.
24. Final System Design Basics Cheat Sheet
Fast reusable copy of expensive data
During partition: strong consistency vs availability
Minimize key movement during membership changes
If you are short on time, revise these first

Distributed-system characteristics -> load balancing + algorithms -> caching -> SQL/NoSQL -> partitioning -> indexing -> replication -> CAP/PACELC -> consistent hashing -> quorum -> leader/follower -> heartbeat -> Bloom filters -> real-time communication.
System Design Trade-offs — Detailed Interview Notes
Section 2 | Deep Coverage of the 23 Trade-off Lessons
The interviewer's real question is usually not 'What technology do you know?' but 'Why is this choice appropriate here?'
Every system design decision has benefits and costs. Explain what you're optimizing and what you're sacrificing.
Simple designs may struggle at scale.
More replicas improve reliability but increase cost.
Longer TTL improves cache hits but increases stale data.
Cache hot URLs for faster redirects and fewer DB reads, accepting stale data risks. Use shorter TTLs if URLs change frequently.
Time taken to process a single request.
Number of requests processed per second.
A service can respond quickly but handle few requests.
Batch processing handles millions of records, but individual records may wait longer.
Over-optimizing p50 while tail latency is bad
Maximizing throughput by creating long queues
p50 = median request latency; half of requests are faster and half slower.
p95 (95th Percentile): 95% of requests complete within this time; 5% take longer.
p99 (99th Percentile): 99% of requests complete within this time; 1% take longer.
: Identify slow requests that average latency may hide.
if one request calls 20 services, one slow dependency can delay the whole request.
higher throughput, but each item may wait for the batch.
less network bandwidth, but adds CPU and encode/decode latency.
lower end-to-end latency, but higher resource usage and load.
improves burst throughput and protects dependencies, but adds waiting latency.

For an interactive API I optimize p95/p99 latency within a required throughput envelope. For offline analytics I can tolerate seconds or minutes of latency if batching significantly increases throughput and lowers cost.
You are early in product life and one database/server has plenty of headroom.
The workload benefits from large memory/local state.
Operational simplicity is more valuable than theoretical infinite scale.
A single node cannot handle peak load or dataset size.
You need fault tolerance across machines/AZs.
'Horizontal scaling is always better.' It introduces distributed state, network failures, replica consistency, data rebalancing, and operational cost.
Vertical Scaling: Upgrade CPU/RAM first; simpler and cheaper initially.
Horizontal Scaling: Add more servers when one server reaches its limits.
Stateless Services: Easy to scale horizontally.
Stateful Databases: Require replication or partitioning to scale.
Forward proxy is on the client side; reverse proxy is on the server side.
Often sees proxy plus forwarded client metadata
A forward proxy represents the client when it talks outward. A reverse proxy represents the server side and becomes the entry point to one or many backend services.
5. CDN Usage vs Direct Server Serving
A CDN is most valuable when reusable content can be served near globally distributed users.
What to Cache at a CDN
Public product/catalog pages or API responses when personalization is absent.
Immutable versioned assets can use very long TTLs.
Highly personalized response for every request.
Small internal application in one geography.
Data changes every request and cannot be cached.
I use a CDN when users are geographically distributed and content is reusable. It lowers latency and origin load, but creates cache-key, TTL, invalidation, and security decisions.
A load balancer distributes traffic; an API gateway adds API-level control and policy.
Yes. API Gateway may route to a private load balancer/service integration.
Public internet -> CDN/WAF -> API Gateway -> internal services is common.
For simple web traffic, ALB alone may be sufficient and cheaper/simpler.
7. API Gateway vs Direct Service Exposure
Direct exposure means clients address a service/load balancer directly. A gateway centralizes cross-cutting API concerns but introduces another network hop and control plane.
Few internal services with trusted clients.
Ultra-low-latency internal RPC where centralized policy would be wasteful.
Service mesh/internal discovery already handles security/routing.
Mobile/external clients should not know internal service topology.
You need one authentication and rate-limit boundary.
Many teams expose APIs and need consistent governance.
A gateway buys central control and decouples clients from service topology. Direct exposure buys simplicity and lower latency. I choose based on how much cross-cutting API policy exists.
Token bucket preserves controlled burst capacity; leaky bucket smooths output.
Allows bursts up to bucket capacity
If idle for 10 seconds, the client can burst up to 100 requests immediately.
After tokens are consumed, sustainable rate returns to ~10/sec.
Atomic updates are required under concurrency.
Clock drift and refill calculations matter.
Per-user, per-IP, per-API-key, and global limits have different cardinality/cost.
Stateless services externalize durable/session state; stateful services keep important context locally.
WebSocket owner, game server, stream processor
Stateless Does Not Mean No State
The application still has state; it lives in DB/cache/object storage/token rather than one app instance's memory.
Externalizing state adds network calls and storage dependencies.

I keep commodity request-processing services stateless when possible because failover and scale-out become easier. I accept stateful ownership when persistent connections or local stream state provide important latency/coordination benefits.
Serverless and long-running compute optimize different workload shapes.
Low-to-medium traffic APIs with bursty demand.
Sustained high utilization where provisioned compute is cheaper.

Serverless is attractive when traffic is bursty and operational simplicity matters. Long-running containers/servers are better when workload is steady, latency must be predictable, or I need deep runtime/control.
REST names resources; RPC names actions/procedures.
Possible but not REST's core strength
Broad HTTP ecosystem and browser/tool support.
Good cache semantics for GET resources.
Efficient serialization and streaming in gRPC.

KGS moves uniqueness work out of the user request and lets app servers reserve codes in batches.

Easy: each campaign/user has distinct code

No search engine — exact key lookup is enough.
Keep analytics off the redirect path.

5. How do you migrate from SQL to sharded KV?

6. How would you handle abuse scanning without SSRF?

7. How do you monitor this system?

12. What consistency can redirect reads use?

13. How do editable links change design?

14. Should the same long URL always return the same code?
Not necessarily. Different users/campaigns/expiry/analytics often need different links. Use idempotency keys for request retries instead of global URL dedupe.
Atomically reserve the requested alias in the same key namespace and return conflict if already used.

41. How to Present This in a 45-Minute Interview
Part VII — Complete follow-up interview bank
Q1. How will you generate short codes without collisions at scale?

Start by separating encoding from ID generation. A Base62 encoder only converts an ID into a compact URL-safe string; uniqueness comes from the underlying ID. For a distributed system, a Snowflake-style 64-bit generator is a strong choice: timestamp + worker identity + sequence produce unique IDs independently on many servers. Base62-encode the generated ID. Alternatives are random Base62 strings with collision checks, or a central counter for a simpler system. Avoid assuming that truncating a hash makes collisions impossible.
Central counter vs distributed ID generation
Base62 does not itself guarantee uniqueness.
A single auto-increment database can become a coordination bottleneck.
Q2. If you use random/hash-based codes and a collision occurs, what do you do?

Enforce a unique constraint on shortCode in the database. Generate a candidate, attempt an atomic insert, and if the unique constraint fails, generate another candidate and retry with a bounded retry policy. The database uniqueness constraint is the final correctness guard. As the namespace fills, collision probability rises, so choose sufficient code length rather than relying on endless retries.
Check-then-insert without a unique constraint is race-prone.
Q3. What should the cache key and value be?

Use shortCode as the cache key because it is exactly what the redirect request provides. Store longUrl as the minimum value; optionally store status, expiresAt, or a version. The redirect service first checks Redis and falls back to the database on a miss, then populates the cache.
Q4. Which cache eviction/expiry strategy would you use?

Use a bounded Redis memory policy appropriate to the workload, commonly LRU/LFU-like behavior, plus TTLs for freshness and memory reclamation. TTLs should be jittered so large groups of entries do not expire simultaneously. If links themselves expire, the cache TTL must never outlive the authoritative expiresAt.
Q5. A URL goes viral and receives millions of hits. How do you handle the hot key?

A single hot key is not solved merely by sharding because all requests for that key still map to one shard/cache owner. Add layers that replicate the value: local in-memory caches on app servers, Redis read replicas where appropriate, and edge/CDN caching for redirects. Protect refill with request coalescing. At extreme scale, replicate the hot object deliberately rather than trying to partition one key.
“Add more shards” does not by itself split traffic for one key.
Q6. What is request coalescing and how does it help here?

When many requests miss the same key concurrently, designate one in-flight request as the leader. Only that request fetches the database value; the others wait for its result. The leader fills Redis and shares the result. This prevents thousands of identical DB reads after one hot key expires. Within one process this is often called single-flight; across processes you need distributed coordination or another shared caching layer.

Instead of giving every cache entry exactly the same TTL, add a small random component, for example baseTTL ± a bounded random amount. That spreads expiration times and reduces a cache avalanche in which many keys become misses simultaneously.
Q8. Walk through the complete redirect flow.

Receive GET /{shortCode}; validate the code; check local cache if present, then Redis. On hit, validate status/expiry and redirect. On Redis miss, route to the correct DB shard using shortCode, fetch the mapping, validate it, populate Redis, emit analytics asynchronously, and return 301 or 302. If absent, return 404; if a previously valid resource is intentionally gone/expired, 410 can be considered depending on API semantics.
Q9. Why use shortCode as a primary key or unique indexed key?

Redirect requests contain shortCode, so indexing directly on it makes the dominant lookup efficient. If the table instead uses an internal ID as the primary key, shortCode still needs a unique secondary index. At large scale, using shortCode as the logical shard key also lets the service route directly to the correct shard.

Use 301 when the destination is truly permanent and you are comfortable with browsers/proxies caching the redirect, reducing future traffic to your service. Use 302 when you want clients to continue contacting the shortener, which preserves control over destination changes and server-side click measurement. Many shorteners favor temporary redirects for control, even when the target rarely changes.
Q11. How would you shard billions of URL mappings?

Hash the shortCode and route based on the hash. Hash sharding avoids the sequential-write hotspot that range-sharding monotonically increasing IDs can create. The mapping should be deterministic so any application server can calculate the destination shard.
Q12. What happens when you add or remove shards?

Simple hash(key) mod N causes widespread remapping when N changes. Consistent hashing maps both keys and shards onto a ring so membership changes move only neighboring key ranges. Virtual nodes place each physical shard at many points on the ring, improving balance and making rebalancing smoother.
Q13. What if one database shard goes down?

Replicate every shard. If the leader fails, promote a healthy replica and update routing/metadata. Reads may continue from replicas if the consistency model permits. The system also needs health checks, automated failover, backups, and a recovery procedure for a full shard loss.
Q14. What about replication lag immediately after creating a URL?

Do not immediately return 404 from a lagging replica. After the primary write succeeds, populate Redis so immediate redirects usually hit cache. For stronger read-after-write behavior, route the creator’s subsequent reads to the leader for a short period, or on replica miss fall back to the primary before declaring the code absent.
Q15. Snowflake is distributed, but what if a server clock moves backward?

NTP reduces drift but the generator must detect rollback. Compare current time to the last timestamp used. If current time is behind, wait until the clock catches up, temporarily reject generation, or use a safe logical/fallback mechanism. Worker IDs must also be unique; two generators using the same worker ID can create duplicates even with correct clocks.
Q16. Are Base62-encoded Snowflake IDs guessable?

Yes. Base62 is reversible encoding, and sequential/time-structured IDs can be enumerable. This is acceptable if short URLs are public identifiers and enumeration is not a security boundary. If unpredictability matters, use cryptographically random codes or an obfuscating permutation/encryption layer before encoding, while still enforcing uniqueness.
Q17. What security and abuse issues exist?

Creation can be abused for spam, phishing, malware, or resource exhaustion; redirects can be brute-forced. Apply rate limits, authentication/API quotas where relevant, URL reputation or malware scanning, domain/block lists, CAPTCHA for anonymous high-risk creation, and monitoring. Treat the short code as an identifier, not an authorization secret unless it is generated with sufficient entropy and the product explicitly relies on secrecy.
Q18. How do you delete a short URL correctly when it may be cached?

Mark/delete the mapping in the authoritative DB and invalidate all relevant cache layers. A tombstone is often safer than immediate physical deletion because it can propagate “this code is gone” and prevent stale replicas/caches from resurrecting it. Multi-region systems may publish an invalidation event and include version/status metadata in cached values.
Q19. How would you deploy this across India, the US, and Europe?

Use global traffic management to route users to nearby healthy regions. Serve redirects from regional caches/replicas for low latency. Choose a write topology: a home/primary region is simpler; multi-leader is more complex. Replicate mappings asynchronously, then handle local replica misses with a fallback to the authoritative region so replication lag does not cause false 404s.
Q20. Won’t falling back to the primary region on every nonexistent code be expensive?

Yes. Cache confirmed “not found” results for a short TTL so repeated invalid codes do not repeatedly cross regions or hit the DB. This is negative caching. Keep the TTL short and invalidate/update it when a code is created; otherwise a newly created mapping can be hidden behind a stale negative entry.
Q21. What if Redis is completely unavailable?

First avoid a single point of failure with Redis replicas/sentinel/cluster or managed failover. During a full cache outage, use local per-instance caches for hottest data, protect the DB with concurrency limits/rate limiting/load shedding, and spread reads across DB replicas where safe. When Redis returns, warm gradually instead of flooding the DB to rebuild the cache.
Q22. A client times out while creating a URL and retries. How do you avoid duplicate creations?

Accept an Idempotency-Key. Atomically claim/store it with the operation and final result. A retry with the same key returns the original short code rather than creating another. Do not automatically deduplicate solely by longUrl unless product requirements say identical long URLs must share a short code.
Q23. Two create requests with the same idempotency key arrive simultaneously. What happens?

Use an atomic uniqueness boundary. A DB row with a unique idempotency-key constraint is robust; Redis SET NX with TTL can also elect one request as the owner. The winner creates and stores the result; losers wait/poll/read the stored result. Ensure the lock does not expire while work is still active, or use a lease-extension/fencing strategy for more rigorous designs.
Q24. How do you record click analytics without slowing redirects?

Keep analytics off the synchronous redirect path. After resolving the URL, publish a small click event to Kafka or another durable queue and return the redirect without waiting for downstream aggregation. Consumers can enrich, aggregate, and persist analytics independently. This decouples redirect availability/latency from analytics storage.
Q25. What if Kafka is down?

Redirect availability should usually win. The producer can retry briefly and/or buffer locally if losing events is unacceptable; otherwise drop some analytics after a bounded attempt. If consumers are down but Kafka is healthy, retained events can be processed later. Design consumers to tolerate duplicates because retries and at-least-once delivery can replay events.
Q26. How do you expire billions of short URLs?

Store expiresAt and index it. Enforce expiry on every redirect read, so correctness never depends on cleanup. A background worker scans the expiry index in bounded batches and tombstones/deletes expired rows. Redis TTL can mirror expiry. Avoid full-table daily scans because they become increasingly expensive.
Q27. What if the expiration cleanup worker is down for hours?

Nothing incorrect should happen. The row may remain physically present, but the redirect handler compares expiresAt with current time and returns an expired/not-found response. Cleanup is storage maintenance, not the mechanism that defines whether the link is valid.
Q28. Two users request the same custom alias at the same time. How do you decide who wins?

Put a unique constraint on alias/shortCode and attempt an atomic insert. Exactly one transaction succeeds; the other receives a uniqueness conflict and returns “alias already taken.” A Redis lock is optional optimization/coordination, but the database uniqueness constraint should remain the correctness guarantee.
Q29. How do you rate limit the create API across many servers?

Keep rate-limit state in a shared low-latency store such as Redis. Use an atomic token-bucket or sliding-window algorithm keyed by user/API key/IP/tenant. Every create consumes capacity; requests beyond the policy receive HTTP 429. Token bucket permits controlled bursts while maintaining a long-term rate.
Q30. What capacity calculations should you be ready to do?

Estimate writes per second from monthly creates, reads per second from the read/write ratio, storage from mappings × bytes per row × retention, cache size from the hot working set, and network bandwidth from average request/response size. For example, 100 million creates/month is roughly 39 writes/s on average (100,000,000 / 2,592,000 seconds). If redirects are 100× writes, average redirect QPS is roughly 3,900; then apply a peak factor rather than designing only for averages.
Clarify scope: create + redirect; ask whether aliases, expiry, analytics, deletion, and auth are required.
Establish scale/read-heavy nature and latency/availability goals.
Choose shortCode generation: Snowflake 64-bit ID → Base62; discuss clock rollback and predictability.
Design mapping schema keyed/indexed by shortCode.
Draw create path and redirect path.
Add Redis cache-aside; discuss hot keys, stampede, avalanche, penetration.
Shard by hash(shortCode); evolve to consistent hashing + virtual nodes.
Replicate shards; discuss failover and replication lag/read-after-write.
Add multi-region routing and primary fallback on local miss.
Cover failures: Redis outage, DB shard outage, Kafka outage.
Finish with idempotency, deletion/invalidation, expiry, analytics, rate limiting, and abuse controls.
Eventual replicas + cache warm / primary fallback for fresh reads
Geo routing + regional cache/replicas + authoritative fallback
expiresAt read-time enforcement + indexed batch cleanup
Distributed token bucket/sliding window in Redis
KGS or random + atomic unique insert
KV at scale; SQL is fine initially
Redirect SLO, cache hit, DB, KGS pool, analytics lag

textRun.content: Design Pastebin - Complete System Design Interview Guide
The core problem is simple; the depth comes from scale, lifecycle, security, and storage choices.

Design a Pastebin-like service where a user submits a block of text and receives a short URL. Anyone with permission to access that URL can retrieve the stored text. The baseline system is read-heavy, but the interview becomes interesting when the interviewer adds expiration, privacy, custom aliases, large pastes, search, analytics, or viral traffic.
Core operation 2: retrieve a paste using a short identifier.
Core operation 3: expire or delete a paste.
Optional: user accounts, private pastes, custom aliases, syntax highlighting, search, analytics, edit/version history.

Do not begin with search, moderation pipelines, multi-region active-active, and version history unless they are requested. First build a correct create/read system, then evolve it as follow-ups arrive.
Raw vs rendered / authenticated private read

Make pastes immutable after creation. Immutability makes CDN caching, cache invalidation, replication, analytics, and viral traffic handling much simpler. Add versioned edits only if the interviewer explicitly asks.
Low p95/p99; most reads under a few hundred ms
High; viral links should survive spikes
Creator should immediately open returned URL
Eventual reads acceptable for public replicas
Escaping, rate limits, moderation, access control
Pastebin is usually read-heavy and mostly immutable. That strongly favors cache/CDN, simple point-key lookup, append-oriented writes, and asynchronous side effects.
Assume the following round numbers for the design discussion:
Average paste size = 10 KB; maximum paste size = 1 MB.

The write QPS is not extreme, but long-term body storage is large and reads dominate writes. That makes cheap blob/object storage plus aggressive caching more valuable than designing a complicated write pipeline.
5. Paste ID Length and Code Space
Using digits + lowercase + uppercase gives 62 possible symbols per character.
Possible sequentially; random collisions become relevant earlier
Very large but URL becomes slightly longer
Sequential numeric IDs encoded in Base62 do not collide.
Random Base62 strings require a unique constraint and collision retry.
If unlisted URLs rely on secrecy, predictable sequential codes are weaker because enumeration becomes easy.

Use 7-character Base62 paste IDs for the interview assumption. If IDs are random, enforce uniqueness atomically in the metadata store. If IDs come from a KGS or sequence, collision checking is unnecessary.
Body, expiry, visibility, language, optional customAlias
HTML page that safely renders escaped content
Serve text/plain, never execute paste contents
Prefer versioning if edits are required
Example logical fields: content, expiresInSeconds/expiresAt, visibility, language, customAlias, idempotencyKey.
Return pasteId, URL, createdAt, expiresAt, and possibly version. HTTP 201 Created is appropriate.
410 Gone: useful if you want to distinguish expired/deleted from never existing.

If clients may retry POST after a timeout, accept an idempotency key for authenticated users. Store the idempotency key -> pasteId mapping for a bounded period so the same logical create does not create multiple pastes.
The dominant access pattern is pasteId -> metadata/body.
Primary lookup key; generated or custom alias
Object key or inline body reference
Make pasteId the partition/primary key for fast point lookups.
Avoid secondary indexes unless a real query requires them.
For authenticated user's 'my pastes' page, add an ownerId + createdAt access path/index or a separate user-paste index.
Do not place full-text search burden on the primary metadata database.
The synchronous path is small; auxiliary work is asynchronous.
Clients access through CDN/edge, WAF, and load balancing.
Metadata store maps pasteId to contentRef + lifecycle/access fields.
Object store keeps large/long-lived body data.
KGS or distributed ID generation supplies unique IDs.

An event stream carries create/delete and view events from the right source: CDN edge events for public CDN-served views and API events for private/direct reads; search/moderation consume their own events.
At small scale, one SQL database can store pasteId and body together. The production-scale design separates metadata and bodies only after storage size, row size, or cost makes that worthwhile.
Return success only after the durable mapping and body exist.
Rule (object-first): Generate candidate ID → store body under a unique no-overwrite object key → atomically claim URL ID in metadata → return URL.
Verify the user (if required) and limit creation requests.
Check content format, size, TTL, visibility, and custom alias.
Use KGS, random ID, UUID, or sequence. A candidate is not authoritative until its URL key is committed.
Upload to a unique immutable object key (for example, uploads/<UUID>), not an unreserved pastes/<candidateId> key. Prevent overwrites with conditional creation where available.
Atomically insert the candidate ID/alias in the authoritative shared URL namespace and point it to the verified object key. Only committed ACTIVE records are readable.
Optionally cache the paste after the database commit.
Return the short URL only after both storage operations succeed.
Trigger moderation, analytics, indexing, and expiry processing.
If the candidate conflicts, keep the uploaded body at its independent object key and retry with a new generated ID. If creation is abandoned, garbage-collect the unreferenced object.
Never overwrite an existing object named for the colliding ID. Generate a fresh candidate and retry the atomic metadata insert (bounded attempts).
Use an idempotency key to prevent duplicate pastes.
Don't fail the request; cache is optional.
Use a transactional outbox or reliable retry mechanism.

Follow-up: How do you guarantee the generated paste ID is unique?

Follow-up: How do private pastes change the design?

Follow-up: How do you support custom aliases?

Treat generated IDs and custom aliases as claims on the same normalized /p/{slug} namespace. Use an authoritative unique insert, reserve system routes, and return 409 on custom alias conflicts. Follow-up: How do you count views?

Follow-up: How do you support full-text search?

Follow-up: What if the maximum paste size is 500 MB?

Follow-up: How do you prevent XSS?

Follow-up: What if the cache is lost?
Correctness remains because cache is not source of truth. Fall back to storage with rate limiting/request coalescing to avoid a thundering herd.
Follow-up: How do you handle a regional outage?

1. Why is Pastebin primarily a read-heavy system, and how does that influence the architecture?

Once a paste is created, it may be read many times while the write happens only once. In our example the read:write ratio is about 10:1, and viral pastes can make the skew much higher. Therefore I optimize the architecture for cheap repeated reads: CDN for public immutable content, L1/L2 caches, point-key metadata lookup, and object storage for durable bodies. I avoid synchronous per-read writes such as updating a view counter in the main row because that would turn a read-heavy system into a hot-write workload.
2. How would you generate short paste IDs, and which approach would you choose?

There are several valid approaches. A database sequence plus Base62 is simplest and guarantees uniqueness but is predictable and introduces a central allocator. Random Base62 codes are decentralized and hard to enumerate, but the metadata store must atomically reject collisions. At larger scale I prefer a Key Generation Service that pre-generates unique 7-character keys and leases blocks to application instances; the create path then consumes a local key without a database collision check. I would choose the simplest method that meets the scale and secrecy requirements and explicitly discuss how I would evolve it.
3. Why use Base62 and how do you choose the code length?

Base62 uses digits, lowercase letters, and uppercase letters, giving 62 choices per character. Seven characters provide about 3.5 trillion possible values, which is far larger than the number of pastes in our assumed workload. The code length is a capacity and security decision: too short risks exhaustion/collisions, while unnecessarily long codes reduce usability. If codes are random, I also care about birthday-style collision probability and keep the occupied fraction of the namespace very low.
4. Why can't the service simply generate a random code, check whether it exists, and then insert it?

A separate 'check then insert' has a race condition. Two application servers can generate the same code, both query before either inserts, both observe that the key is absent, and then both try to claim it. The storage layer must provide an atomic uniqueness primitive such as a unique primary key or conditional put. If the insert conflicts, one request generates a new code and retries.
5. What is the purpose of a Key Generation Service, and how do you make it scalable?

KGS moves ID uniqueness work out of the paste-create hot path. It maintains a pool of unique keys and leases blocks of keys to paste-service instances, so an instance can create many pastes using only local memory. The KGS should allocate blocks atomically, replicate its allocator state, and maintain a large safety buffer. If a paste-service instance dies, I would rather waste its unused leased keys than risk reissuing them, because the key namespace is huge and duplicate IDs are a correctness failure.
6. Would you store the paste body in the database or in object storage?

For a small system, storing the body inline with metadata in SQL is the cleanest design because one transaction creates the paste and one lookup reads it. At larger scale, body storage grows much faster than metadata and bodies can be large, so I prefer a small metadata row plus an immutable object in object storage. That keeps database rows/indexes compact and uses a storage system optimized for durable blobs. The cost is an extra lookup and cross-store lifecycle management, so I would not split them prematurely.
7. How do you order the object-store and metadata writes so partial failures are safe?

For object-first writes, upload to a unique, no-overwrite staging/object key independent of the uncommitted candidate pasteId; then atomically insert ACTIVE metadata linking the claimed ID to that key. On collision, retry the ID without overwriting the existing body. An orphan object is cleanable, but visible metadata must never reference a missing body. For direct pre-signed uploads, reserve PENDING metadata first and publish only after verifying the object.
8. What database would you choose for the metadata store?

The dominant access pattern is an exact lookup by pasteId, so both SQL and distributed key-value databases fit. I would start with a relational database for moderate scale because it provides simple uniqueness constraints, transactions, and operational familiarity. At very large scale, a partitioned key-value store keyed by pasteId is natural because queries are simple and easy to distribute. The decision should be based on the required write scale, multi-region model, operational expertise, and consistency guarantees rather than the label SQL versus NoSQL.
9. How would you partition the metadata database?

I would hash-partition by pasteId. The IDs are high-cardinality and, if generated randomly or by a well-distributed allocator, spread traffic evenly. Each normal read or write touches one partition, which is exactly what we want. I would not partition by creation time because recent writes could create a hot shard, and I would create separate derived indexes for owner history or search rather than compromise the primary partition key.
10. How do you guarantee read-after-create if replicas are asynchronous?

After a successful create, an asynchronous read replica may not have the new metadata yet. I can solve this by reading from the primary for the creator's session, by warming the distributed cache after the authoritative commit, or by attaching a version/session token and refusing a replica that is behind. I do not need global strong consistency for every public read; I only need the user-visible guarantee that the URL I just returned works immediately.
11. How would you design the cache?

I would use cache-aside. Each API instance can have a small L1 in-process cache for the hottest entries and a shared L2 distributed cache for the broader working set. Cache keys should include pasteId and version if edits exist, and the TTL must never outlive the paste expiration time. On a miss the service loads metadata/body from durable storage and fills the cache. I would also use request coalescing and TTL jitter to protect the origin from stampedes.
12. Why is a CDN especially effective for Pastebin?

Public immutable pastes are highly cacheable and can become viral. A CDN serves content from edge locations close to users and absorbs huge spikes without sending each request to the application, cache cluster, or database. It also reduces global latency and origin egress pressure. However, private content must not enter a public reusable cache, and deletion/takedown semantics require either bounded TTLs or explicit purge/invalidation.
13. How do you handle one paste that suddenly receives millions of requests per second?

This is a hot-key problem, not a normal average-QPS problem. I would serve the paste from CDN, keep it in L1 caches across many API instances, replicate the shared cache entry where possible, and coalesce any origin miss so only one request fetches the body. I would not synchronously update a single view counter for every request because that creates another hot key. The origin should also have concurrency limits and circuit breakers so a CDN/cache failure cannot take down storage.
14. How should paste expiration work at large scale?

The read path should always check expiresAt and refuse to serve expired content. Physical deletion can be asynchronous: a sweeper or database TTL mechanism removes metadata later, and object-storage lifecycle rules delete the body. This avoids running one timer for every paste and keeps correctness independent from cleanup timing. Cache TTLs must be capped at the remaining paste lifetime so stale expired content is not served.
15. What is the difference between an unlisted paste and a private paste?

An unlisted paste is discoverability-based security: it is not listed/searchable, but anyone who knows the random URL can access it. A private paste has an actual authorization rule, such as owner-only or an ACL, and the service must authenticate and authorize every read. Random high-entropy IDs are useful for unlisted content but should never be presented as equivalent to access control. I would also keep private content out of public CDN caches and public search indexes.
16. How would you implement delete so a stale cache does not keep serving the paste?

I would first update the authoritative metadata state to DELETED, then invalidate or purge L1/L2/CDN entries, and finally delete the body asynchronously according to retention policy. Reads check metadata status or use cache entries with bounded TTLs, so deletion eventually reaches all layers. If takedown must be near-instant, the CDN needs an explicit purge mechanism and caches should not use very long immutable TTLs without purge support. For regulated content, I would define and monitor a deletion-propagation SLO.
17. What changes if pastes can be edited?

I would avoid in-place mutation of the body and instead create immutable versions. A small metadata record points to currentVersion, and each body is stored under pasteId/version. Updates use optimistic concurrency such as expectedVersion to prevent lost writes. This design keeps old bodies cacheable, provides history/rollback, and makes CDN/cache invalidation easier because a versioned URL never changes.
18. How would you add full-text search?

I would not put search queries on the primary paste metadata database. PasteCreated and PasteDeleted events feed an asynchronous indexer that writes only PUBLIC pastes into a dedicated search engine/inverted index. Search results can be eventually consistent because they are a discovery feature, but when a user opens a result the Paste API still rechecks current status and authorization. This prevents a stale search document from bypassing a recent deletion or privacy change.
19. How would you collect view counts and analytics without hurting read latency?

Keep reads independent of analytics. Count public reads at the CDN edge (hits and misses) because API-only events miss CDN hits; count private/direct API reads at the API. Send those events to Kafka/queue, deduplicate deliveries and prevent double counting on edge misses, then aggregate view counts and trends in an OLAP store. Never increment the primary paste row synchronously. If analytics is unavailable, reads still succeed; telemetry may be delayed or dropped per policy.
20. What are the main security risks in a Pastebin-like service?

The biggest application risk is untrusted content. Rendered views must HTML-escape paste contents, raw responses should be text/plain, and a strict Content Security Policy reduces script execution risk. Anonymous creation also attracts spam, phishing, malware indicators, scraping, and denial-of-service traffic, so I need rate limits, size limits, WAF rules, abuse reporting, and moderation workflows. Private pastes additionally need real authentication/authorization and careful logging that never dumps sensitive bodies.
21. How would you handle very large pastes or files?

Once paste sizes reach hundreds of megabytes, routing the entire payload through stateless API servers becomes inefficient. I would create an upload session, return a pre-signed object-storage URL, let the client upload directly, and then finalize metadata only after verifying the object. Multipart upload supports large bodies, and asynchronous scanning can run before public publication. The API becomes a control plane rather than a bulk-data proxy.
22. How does the design change for multi-region active-active writes?

Global reads are relatively easy because public content can be CDN-cached and metadata/object data can be replicated. Writes are harder because paste IDs and custom aliases must remain unique. Generated IDs can use disjoint KGS blocks per region or a region/worker-aware distributed ID, while custom alias creation may need a globally consistent coordinator or a single owning region. I would only choose fully active-active writes if the write-latency requirement justifies the extra conflict and consistency complexity.
23. What happens if the cache cluster goes down?

The cache is an optimization, so correctness should not depend on it. Requests fall back to metadata and object storage, but that can suddenly multiply origin load, so I would use request coalescing, rate limits, circuit breakers, and gradual cache warm-up. Capacity planning should assume at least a partial cache-loss scenario. The service may temporarily run at reduced throughput, but it should not return incorrect content.
24. What happens if the KGS is unavailable?

Paste-service instances should already hold leased blocks of unused IDs in memory or local durable state. They continue creating pastes from that reserve while the KGS is repaired. Monitoring alerts when local pools fall below a safe threshold. If all key pools are exhausted, new creates may fail while reads remain fully available; I prefer that to generating unsafe duplicate IDs.
25. Why not store the view counter, search text, body, owner history, and everything else in one database row?

Those features have different access and scaling patterns. The primary metadata row is optimized for pasteId point lookup and lifecycle checks, object storage is optimized for large immutable bodies, search uses an inverted index, and analytics uses append/aggregate workloads. Forcing all of them into one store couples unrelated traffic and makes viral reads or analytics writes contend with the critical create/read path. Separation is justified when the scale appears; a small V1 can still start with one database.
26. How do you prevent enumeration attacks against unlisted pastes?

Use high-entropy random IDs rather than sequential codes, keep the code space much larger than the number of active pastes, rate-limit clients that generate many 404s, and short-term negative-cache nonexistent IDs. However, I would clearly state that this only makes guessing difficult. If disclosure would be harmful, the paste should be PRIVATE and require authentication/authorization rather than relying on an unguessable URL.
27. How would you make paste creation idempotent?

For authenticated or API clients, accept an idempotency key with the create request. Store idempotencyKey -> pasteId together with a request fingerprint for a bounded period. If the client retries after a timeout, return the original paste instead of creating a duplicate; if the same idempotency key is reused with a different payload, reject it. This is especially important when the server committed the paste but the response was lost.
28. What would you monitor first in production?

I would start with user-facing read and write success rate, p95/p99 latency, and SLO burn. Then I would monitor cache/CDN hit ratio, metadata and object-store errors/latency, KGS key-pool depth, expiry/delete propagation, and asynchronous backlog. Logs/traces should identify whether slow reads came from cache misses, metadata, or object storage. I would avoid logging full paste contents, especially for private content.
29. How would you explain the final design in one sentence?

It is a read-optimized immutable-content service: stateless APIs create a globally unique short pasteId, store small lifecycle metadata in a point-key database and the body in durable blob storage, then serve public reads through CDN/L1/L2 caches while asynchronous streams handle analytics, moderation, search, and cleanup. The architecture keeps the critical create/read path small and separates lifecycle/security correctness from optional derived features.
30. What is the most important trade-off in this problem?

The most important design theme is simplicity versus read-scale optimization. A single relational database can solve the basic problem correctly, but at large scale we introduce object storage, caches, CDN, KGS, and async pipelines because the workload is immutable, read-heavy, and potentially viral. Each extra component should be justified by a bottleneck or requirement; otherwise it only increases operational complexity.

4. Why should cache TTL never exceed paste expiry?

5. Why does sharding not solve a viral paste?

6.3 Sliding Window Counter: approximate rolling count

The requirement is a sustained request rate with a controlled short burst. Token Bucket expresses that with a refill rate and capacity, supports request costs, and keeps constant state per active subject.
Why not a local counter in every gateway?
Each gateway gives another independent allowance; load balancing multiplies the effective limit. I use one shared owner or deliberately divided reserved quotas.

Is Redis Lua enough for global exactness?
No. It serializes decisions on one executing owner. It does not by itself solve cross-slot transactions, replication-loss failover or globally coordinated multi-region rules.
Outcome is unknown: it may have consumed and lost the reply. I apply this rule’s outage policy; exact replay needs an atomic saved decision ID/result.
What if the user bucket denies after tenant allows?
Sequential charging can spend the tenant token. I state that as attempt/conservative charging, or colocate related buckets for joint check-and-consume when admitted-only semantics are required.
How do you handle a global hot key?
One key remains serialized on one owner despite normal sharding. I can isolate it, or reserve regional/gateway token grants if the required quota semantics allow delegation.
An asynchronous promoted replica may miss recent consumption, restoring permission. I explicitly state the tolerance or use stronger recovery measures for strict rules.
Why separate rate and concurrency limits?
Rate bounds starts over time, but 60-second tasks can still pile up. Concurrency permits bound in-flight resource usage.
How do clients recover from a 429?
Honor Retry-After when supplied, add jitter/backoff, bound attempts, and use business request idempotency for non-idempotent retries.
Why not one global limiter DB?
Global per-request coordination adds WAN round trips and a partition dependency. Regional grants reduce latency at the cost of utilization and precisely bounded failure/policy-change semantics.
How do you know the limiter is working?
Track user-visible error/denial patterns, decision p99, Redis health, key skew, config-version lag and rule-specific fallback; test with controlled clocks and parallel histories.

29.1 A Few More Interview Questions Worth Practicing
Why not a normal SQL table for every API hit?
Every request would add a durable write with index/lock cost to a latency-sensitive path. In-memory atomic counters are faster for protective quotas; use durable storage separately for paid credits.
What if two requests arrive at exactly the same timestamp?
An atomic owner decides their order. For a sliding log, store a unique member per request as well as the timestamp score so one request cannot overwrite another.
How do you choose bucket capacity?
Capacity is the maximum saved burst. Size it from backend headroom and desired behavior, not only the refill rate. Large capacity may allow a burst the service cannot survive.
What is rate limiting at edge versus gateway?
Edge limits block coarse IP/device abuse before origin. Gateway limits can use authenticated user, tenant, method and route context for business policies.
Is a per-user rate limit equal to a per-IP rate limit?
No. A shared NAT IP can group legitimate users, and users may change addresses. Prefer authenticated identity for product limits and IP for coarse abuse.
Why are all Redis reads not safe from replicas?

28. Cache Node Failure, Recovery and Cold-Start Storms
Cache miss/failure fallbacks must be limited to protect the database.
1. Detect unhealthy node using health checks/timeouts; stop routing new requests to it.
2. Switch to a healthy replica or updated shard owner if available.
3. If no cached copy exists, fall back to database but cap concurrent origin requests.
4. Refill the recovering/new node gradually; avoid sending all keys for immediate reload.
5. Rebalance only after membership changes are confirmed; prevent routing flaps.
If a cache absorbs 95% of 200k reads/s, database load may jump from ~10k to ~200k reads/s during a complete outage. That can trigger a cascading failure even though the database was healthy before.

A restarted shard is cold. Flooding it with every possible key immediately consumes bandwidth and may also flood the backing database. 29. Failure Detection: Health Checks and Gossip
A distributed cluster needs to discover when a machine is unhealthy, and everyone needs a reasonably consistent membership view before sending keys to it.
Nodes exchange heartbeat/membership updates with a few peers, not every peer.
1. Each node tracks a membership list with node IDs, heartbeat counters and last-seen times.
2. Periodically it updates its own heartbeat and shares selected health records with random peers.
3. Peers forward newer information so membership changes spread through the cluster.
4. A node with a missing heartbeat becomes suspect; corroborating probes or peer evidence reduce false failure declarations.
5. Once the cluster confirms a failure, routing and replica placement update in a controlled way.
All-to-all health messaging grows expensive as node count increases. Gossip reduces direct communication while spreading cluster state.
A slow machine or brief network pause does not necessarily mean a permanent crash. Avoid constant member flapping.
Centralized health checks can be sufficient for a managed cache; gossip is a useful decentralized design follow-up.
