textRun.content: Design Google Search / Web Search Engine
Complete Advanced System Design Interview Guide
Problem 21 | Crawling, Indexing, Ranking, Query Serving & Freshness

Design a large-scale web search engine that continuously discovers and crawls the public web, processes and deduplicates documents, builds distributed indexes, ranks results, and answers queries with very low latency. This is a pipeline-heavy system: crawling and indexing are asynchronous, while query serving is latency-critical.

Given billions of web pages and a continuous stream of changes, build a system that discovers pages, downloads them politely, extracts useful content and links, constructs a searchable index, and returns high-quality top results for user queries in a fraction of a second.

Search is two giant systems joined together: an offline/nearline ingestion pipeline that converts the web into indexes, and an online distributed query engine that retrieves and ranks a tiny top-K from enormous immutable index data.
Search public web pages, not private enterprise documents.
Support keyword/text queries; semantic/vector retrieval can be an extension.
Return title, URL, snippet, and ranked result list.
Crawler must obey robots rules and host politeness.
Index should refresh continuously; different pages have different recrawl frequencies.
Exact Google ranking is out of scope; design ranking architecture and representative signals.
Autocomplete/spelling can be follow-ups but are included.
Ads, image/video search, and personalized search are optional extensions.

I’ll separate the system into crawl/index and query-serving planes. The crawl plane uses a durable URL frontier with per-host politeness, fetchers, parsing, duplicate detection, link extraction, and an incremental indexing pipeline. The serving plane shards an inverted index, retrieves candidates in parallel, merges top-K, applies ranking, and uses aggressive caching.
Find new URLs from seeds and extracted links
Parse, normalize, detect duplicates, extract links/text
Recrawl changing pages and update index
Minutes to days by page class
Do not obsess over exact Google numbers. Show that crawling, storage, indexing, and serving each operate at different scales, and that query serving cannot scan documents at request time.
Normalize scheme/host case and default ports.
Resolve relative links and dot segments.
Apply safe URL normalization rules without incorrectly merging distinct resources.
Remove fragments because they usually do not change server resource.
Treat tracking parameters carefully; use learned/rule-based canonical hints rather than blindly deleting every query parameter.
Respect page-provided canonical URLs as a signal, not unquestioned truth.
Store URL fingerprint for fast seen checks.
Without canonicalization, the crawler wastes bandwidth fetching many syntactic URLs for the same logical page and pollutes the index with duplicates.
8. URL Frontier: The Heart of the Crawler
The frontier is not a simple FIFO queue. It decides what to crawl next while balancing priority, freshness, fairness, and per-host politeness.
Front-end priority queues rank important/fresh URLs.
Back-end queues group work by host/domain to enforce politeness.
Each host has next_allowed_fetch_time and concurrency budget.
Scheduler chooses a ready host, then one URL from that host.
Durably checkpoint frontier state; losing it should not reset the crawl.
Important pages should be discovered/refreshed sooner
News/homepages change faster than archival pages
A practical score combines importance, expected change probability, staleness, host health, and crawl budget.
Fetch and cache robots.txt per host with expiry.
Limit concurrent requests per host/domain/IP as policy requires.
Maintain next allowed fetch time and exponential backoff on errors.
Use adaptive crawl rate based on server latency/errors.
Bound URLs per host/day to prevent traps and one site consuming the fleet.
Identify crawler via user agent and honor standard directives.
A crawler that maximizes throughput but overloads websites is badly designed. Host politeness is a first-class scheduling invariant.
Stateless fetch workers lease URLs from ready frontier partitions.
DNS, TLS, redirects, compression, timeouts, content-length limits, and MIME checks are handled defensively.
Redirect destination is canonicalized and re-enters frontier if eligible.
Record status, headers, ETag/Last-Modified, content hash, latency, and crawl timestamp.
Conditional GET can reduce bandwidth on recrawl.
Large/binary/non-indexable content routes to specialized pipelines or is skipped.
Fetcher acknowledges lease only after durable fetch metadata/content handoff.
Infinite calendars/session IDs/query combinations can generate unbounded URLs.
Detect repeated URL patterns and excessive path/query cardinality.
Limit depth and per-site URL budgets.
Content fingerprinting detects pages that differ only superficially.
Spam/malware classifiers can lower crawl/index priority.
Sandbox parsers; never execute arbitrary page code in privileged crawler infrastructure.
Use rendering/headless-browser tier only for pages that need JavaScript, because it is far more expensive than HTTP fetch.
Clean text, fields, language, canonical URL
Keep raw and processed data separate
Reprocessing parsers/ranking features should not require recrawling the internet. Durable raw snapshots let you rebuild downstream artifacts.
Extract title, visible text, headings, anchors, structured metadata, language, and links.
Assign stable doc_id and emit processed document + link events.
Exact duplicates: cryptographic/content hash after normalization.
Near duplicates: SimHash/MinHash or shingles to detect highly similar pages.
Choose one representative/canonical document for result display.
Duplicate groups reduce index size and improve result diversity.
Do not merge merely because URLs look similar; compare content and canonical signals.
Dedupe can happen during crawl to save work and again during result serving for diversity.
URL dedupe prevents refetching the same URL; content dedupe prevents indexing many URLs with the same or nearly identical content.
Extracted links form a massive directed graph. Offline graph processing can derive authority/importance features similar in spirit to PageRank.
Anchor text is useful evidence about destination content.
Compute global or topical authority scores in batch/iterative jobs.
Handle spam/link farms with quality signals.
Graph score is only one ranking feature; query relevance remains essential.
Incremental graph updates can coexist with periodic full recomputation.
Search serving depends primarily on the inverted index: instead of scanning billions of documents, retrieve only postings for query terms.
Inverted index: term dictionary to compressed postings
Dictionary maps normalized term to postings metadata/offset.
Posting contains doc_id delta, term frequency, field flags, optional positions.
Sort doc IDs and delta/varint/compress postings to reduce I/O.
Skip blocks/max-score metadata allow query engine to avoid scanning every posting.
Positions support phrase/proximity queries but increase index size.
Processed docs are partitioned into indexing batches/streams.
Tokenizer emits (term, doc_id, field, position) records.
Build immutable index segments with dictionaries, postings, document metadata, and statistics.
Serving replicas load/map new segment generation.
Background compaction merges small segments and applies tombstones.
Atomic generation pointer makes new index version visible.
Readers can query a stable generation without locks while new segments are built separately. Publication is a metadata pointer change; compaction happens in background.
New/changed documents enter small fresh index segments quickly.
Large base index changes less frequently.
Query serving searches base + fresh segments and merges results.
Periodic compaction folds fresh segments into larger optimized segments.
Deletion/takedown tombstones suppress documents immediately before physical compaction.
Freshness tier may prioritize news/high-change sources.
21. Index Sharding: Document vs Term Partitioning
Each shard indexes subset of docs and all terms
Query fans to all shards; easy balanced corpus
Document-shard the corpus. Each shard computes its local top-K for the query, then an aggregator merges shard winners. Replicate shards for availability and query throughput.
Distributed query serving and top-K merge
Normalize query, detect language, spelling, intent/safe-search policy.
Planner selects index generation/shards and query operators.
Fan query to one healthy replica of every required document shard.
Each shard retrieves postings, intersects/unions terms, scores candidates, returns local top-K.
Aggregator merges local top-K into global candidate set.
Optional expensive reranker applies richer features.
Return results and asynchronously log impression/click telemetry.
Stopword handling is language/query dependent; do not blindly remove meaningful words.
Query intent/entity understanding can enrich ranking but should degrade gracefully.
For a multi-term query, retrieve postings lists and combine them efficiently.
AND/intersection: start with shortest/rarest postings list.
OR: merge postings while scoring matching terms.
Phrase: intersect docs then verify positions.
Skip pointers/block metadata jump over impossible ranges.
Use document-at-a-time or term-at-a-time evaluation depending engine.
Early termination avoids fully evaluating candidates that cannot enter top-K.
Find thousands of plausible docs cheaply
Representative features: BM25-like relevance, title/anchor matches, authority, freshness, language/location, page quality, spam score, structured data.
Keep expensive features for a small candidate set.
Ranking models must be versioned and observable.
Do not claim PageRank alone determines search order.
BM25 is a common lexical relevance baseline: reward query terms that appear in a document, give more weight to rare terms, saturate repeated occurrences, and normalize for document length.
You usually do not need to derive the equation. Explain term frequency, inverse document frequency, document-length normalization, and why lexical score is combined with other quality signals.
Each shard returns only its local best K or K' candidates, not all matches.
Aggregator uses a heap/partial sort to merge shard candidates.
K' may be larger than final K to leave room for global reranking/diversity.
Score calibration/statistics must be compatible across shards.
Advanced engines use upper bounds such as block-max scores/WAND-like pruning to skip candidates that cannot beat current threshold.
A common mistake is to say 'sort all matching documents'. Search engines aggressively avoid scoring and transferring candidates that cannot reach the first result page.
Store document text/term offsets or a compact snippet source.
Choose windows around matched query terms.
Prefer coherent sentences/fields and highlight matches.
Precompute static description where dynamic snippet is unnecessary.
Generate snippets only for final top results, not millions of candidates.
Head queries benefit enormously from result caching.
Long-tail queries rely on efficient shard retrieval.
Include policy/locale/index-version dimensions to prevent incorrect reuse.
Invalidate by generation rather than individually expiring every query after index publication where possible.
Estimate how often each page changes from historical observations.
High-importance, frequently changing pages recrawl quickly.
Stable pages back off to days/weeks.
HTTP ETag/Last-Modified can avoid downloading unchanged bodies.
Failures increase backoff; successful changes may shorten interval.
Crawl budget is finite: freshness is an optimization problem.
Serving layer checks tombstones or loads them into shard filters so removal is fast.
Async compaction physically removes postings later.
Legal/safety takedowns should not wait for ordinary recrawl/index cycles.
Build prefix suggestions from historical queries/entities with frequency and quality filters.
Trie/FST or prefix index stores top suggestions per prefix.
Precompute popular prefix top-N to make serving tiny and fast.
Personalization, if any, should be a small overlay rather than scanning history on each keystroke.
Use dictionary/edit-distance candidates, query logs, language models, and entity dictionaries.
Only generate a small candidate set.
Score correction using frequency/context; avoid overcorrecting rare proper nouns.
Can search original and corrected query in parallel for confidence-sensitive cases.
Modern search may combine lexical retrieval with embedding/vector retrieval.
Store vectors in approximate nearest-neighbor indexes.
Retrieve semantic candidates and union with lexical candidates.
Lexical remains valuable for exact names, rare tokens, freshness, and explainability.
Vector index freshness/cost is a separate trade-off.
Each logical document shard has multiple serving replicas.
Query router chooses healthy replica based on latency/load.
Immutable index generations make replica deployment straightforward.
A query may tolerate one missing shard with degraded partial results, but monitor and retry within latency budget.
Hedged requests can reduce tail latency for slow shard replicas.
Keep enough spare capacity for replica loss and rolling index loads.
A distributed query is only as fast as its slowest required shard.
Hedged requests to alternate replica after a small delay.
Return graceful partial/degraded results if policy permits instead of waiting indefinitely.
Median shard latency is not enough. Fan-out to hundreds/thousands of partitions amplifies tail latency, so p99 behavior and straggler mitigation become central.
Durable partition/replica restores queues and host state
Do not publish generation; retry missing segments
Serve older base with reduced freshness
All terms for subset of docs
Crawler can be geographically distributed but must coordinate host politeness; avoid multiple regions hammering one host independently.
Index building may happen in several compute regions, publishing immutable generations to serving regions.
Query serving is active-active close to users.
Replicate complete serving index sets or region-appropriate copies to each search region.
Query logs/telemetry stream to analytics pipelines asynchronously.
Global index generation metadata controls rollout; canary new generations before full activation.
Deletion/takedown propagation receives priority across all regions.
Sandbox parsing/rendering of untrusted web content.
Protect crawler from decompression bombs, giant files, redirect loops, SSRF-like internal address access, and malformed formats.
Spam classifiers detect keyword stuffing, cloaking, link farms, malware, and low-quality pages.
Safe-search/content policies apply at indexing and serving.
Query endpoints need rate limits and abuse controls.
Never let arbitrary crawled HTML execute in search frontend.
Crawler discovers https://example.com/distributed-systems from an existing page.
Canonicalizer normalizes URL; seen store says it is new.
Frontier assigns priority and places it in example.com host bucket.
At next allowed host time, fetcher downloads page and records HTTP metadata.
Parser extracts title, body terms, language, canonical URL, and outgoing links.
Document processor assigns doc_id and emits terms/link graph data.
Incremental indexer creates postings such as 'distributed' → doc_id.
Fresh segment publishes to serving shards.
User searches 'distributed systems'. Query frontend fans to doc shards.
Shard containing the document retrieves/scorers it; global aggregator merges top-K.
Reranker applies authority/freshness/quality; snippet generator extracts matching sentence.
Result is returned and impression/click telemetry feeds future quality analysis.
Durable priority/politeness URL frontier controls crawl work.
Stateless fetchers download pages with robots, rate limits, redirects, timeouts, and conditional requests.
Raw content is stored durably; parsing extracts clean text, metadata, canonical URLs, and links.
Link graph and offline jobs compute static quality/authority signals.
Incremental indexing creates immutable compressed inverted-index segments; background compaction builds optimized generations.
Document-sharded serving replicas answer queries in parallel.
Each shard retrieves and scores local candidates with early termination; aggregator merges global top-K and reranks a small set.
Caches, spell correction, autocomplete, snippets, safety, and semantic retrieval surround the core query path.
Adaptive recrawl scheduling balances freshness, importance, change rate, and host budgets.
Active-active query regions serve users close to them; immutable generations and replicas provide safe rollout/failover.

Continuously turn the web into versioned immutable inverted indexes using a polite priority crawler and incremental processing pipeline, then answer each query by parallel retrieval across replicated document shards, aggressively prune to local top-K, globally merge/rerank, and use adaptive recrawling plus small fresh segments to keep results current.
Document is simpler for distributed top-K
Treating the crawler as a single queue and ignoring host politeness.
Not distinguishing URL dedupe from content dedupe.
Scanning document storage for queries instead of using an inverted index.
Saying 'use Elasticsearch' without designing index construction/sharding/query flow.
Sorting all matching documents instead of distributed top-K/early termination.
Ignoring index freshness and incremental segments.
Rebuilding the entire index for every update.
Not explaining document vs term sharding.
Ignoring p99 tail latency from shard fan-out.
Using PageRank as the entire ranking algorithm.
Ignoring crawl traps, robots.txt, or adversarial pages.

Discover URL → canonicalize/seen check → priority/polite frontier → fetch → parse/dedupe/link extraction → incremental inverted index → replicated document shards → query parse → parallel retrieval → local top-K → global merge/rerank → snippets/results. Deep dives: frontier, inverted index, sharding, top-K, freshness, and tail latency.
Follow-up: Why isn't the URL frontier just Kafka/FIFO?

Answer: Because crawl order depends on priority, host readiness, robots policy, recrawl deadlines, and fairness. A log can be part of durability, but scheduling needs explicit per-host/time structures.
Follow-up: How do you prevent overloading a website?
Answer: Group URLs by host, track next_allowed_fetch_time/concurrency, honor robots, adapt rate to latency/errors, and enforce crawl budgets.
Follow-up: How do you detect that a URL was already crawled?
Answer: Canonicalize it and check a scalable fingerprint/URL metadata store. Bloom filters can reduce expensive lookups but need a durable source of truth because false positives exist.
Follow-up: What if two different URLs have identical content?
Answer: Content hashing/near-duplicate detection groups them; choose a canonical representative and suppress redundant results.
Answer: So parser/tokenizer/ranking changes can reprocess content without recrawling external sites.
Follow-up: What is an inverted index?
Answer: A mapping from term to a compressed postings list of documents containing that term, with statistics/positions needed for retrieval and scoring.
Answer: Each shard owns a subset of docs and all terms for those docs, so it can independently compute local top-K. The query aggregator merges shard winners.
Follow-up: Does every query hit every shard?
Answer: In a basic document-sharded architecture yes, one replica per shard. Tiering/routing/cache/learned techniques can reduce work, but the baseline is parallel fan-out.
Follow-up: How do you handle a very common term?
Answer: Compressed postings, skip/block metadata, conjunction with rarer terms, early termination/WAND-like pruning, and hot-block caching.
Follow-up: How do you update the index without downtime?
Answer: Build immutable fresh segments/generations separately, load them into replicas, then atomically switch generation metadata. Compact later.
Follow-up: How do you delete a page quickly?
Answer: Publish a high-priority tombstone/filter to serving shards and caches immediately; physical index removal occurs during compaction.
Follow-up: How do you rank results?
Answer: Use multi-stage ranking: cheap lexical/static scoring to retrieve candidates, global merge, then richer reranking with relevance, authority, freshness, quality, safety, and other signals.
Follow-up: Why not run the expensive model on every matching page?
Answer: There may be millions of matches. Retrieve a small high-recall candidate set cheaply and spend expensive compute only on the top candidates.
Follow-up: How do you keep results fresh?
Answer: Adaptive recrawl plus small incremental index segments. High-change/high-value pages are recrawled quickly; stable pages back off.
Follow-up: How do you know when to recrawl?
Answer: Historical change rate, importance, last crawl age, sitemaps/feed hints, HTTP validators, and host health determine next deadline.
Follow-up: What causes search tail latency?
Answer: A query fans out to many shards; one slow replica can delay the whole result. Use deadlines, hedged requests, load-aware routing, caching, and bounded reranking.
Follow-up: How does autocomplete differ from search?
Answer: Autocomplete is a prefix top-N problem and is heavily precomputed/cached, often using trie/FST-like structures; it should return in tens of milliseconds.
Follow-up: How would semantic search fit?
Answer: Create document embeddings asynchronously, ANN-retrieve semantic candidates, union them with lexical candidates, and rerank the combined set.
Follow-up: How do you recover a failed index build?
Answer: Segments/generations are immutable and unpublished until complete. Retry failed jobs; the serving fleet keeps using the previous valid generation.
Follow-up: How do you scale globally?
Answer: Replicate serving indexes to active-active query regions, keep immutable generations synchronized, distribute crawling/index computation, and prioritize global deletion propagation.
1. What are the two main systems inside web search?
Answer: A crawl/index pipeline and an online query-serving engine.
2. What is the most important crawler invariant?
Answer: Politeness: never schedule requests in a way that overloads a host or violates robots policy.
Answer: They make host-specific delay, concurrency, backoff, and fairness enforceable.
4. How do you avoid infinite crawl traps?
Answer: URL-pattern detection, per-site budgets, depth limits, duplicate fingerprints, and quality policies.
5. What is the difference between recrawl and discovery?
Answer: Discovery finds previously unknown URLs; recrawl schedules known URLs again to refresh changed content.
6. How is a stable doc_id useful?
Answer: It decouples serving/index references from mutable URLs and lets multiple index generations refer to consistent document metadata.
Answer: Postings dominate index size and I/O. Sorted doc IDs have small deltas that compress extremely well.
Answer: Phrase/proximity queries and better snippet/relevance features; omit or compress them when cost outweighs value.
9. How does a shard find top results?
Answer: Retrieve relevant postings, combine them, score viable candidates, prune using score upper bounds, and keep a small heap of local top-K.
Answer: Merge local K' lists from shards, normalize/apply global features, then rerank and keep final K.
11. What if one shard times out?
Answer: Retry/hedge to replica within deadline; if product permits, return degraded partial results and log the missing shard.
12. Why are immutable segments operationally attractive?
Answer: No reader locks, easy replication/cache, atomic publication, deterministic rollback, and background compaction.
13. How do you prevent stale caches after index updates?
Answer: Version cache keys by index generation or keep short/controlled TTLs; new generation naturally creates new cache namespace.
14. How do you handle news freshness?
Answer: High-priority recrawl feeds a fast incremental index tier that query serving searches alongside the base corpus.
15. Can PageRank be calculated online per query?
Answer: No. Global graph authority is typically computed offline/nearline and stored as a static feature used during query scoring.
16. What is query-independent vs query-dependent ranking?
Answer: Authority/page quality can be precomputed independent of query; lexical relevance, phrase match, and intent match depend on the query.
17. Why does search use multiple ranking stages?
Answer: Cost. Early stages process many candidates with cheap features; later stages process few candidates with expensive models.
Answer: Crawl/index classifiers, graph/content signals, policy systems, and serving-time quality filters. No single signal is sufficient.
19. What should remain available if ranking ML fails?
Answer: Lexical retrieval plus static quality/freshness ranking should provide a useful fallback.

Answer: Priority/polite crawler feeds durable processing and dedupe; incremental immutable inverted indexes are replicated by document shard; query frontends fan out in parallel, each shard computes local top-K, and a global aggregator reranks a small candidate set while caches and adaptive recrawl control latency and freshness.
1. Why isn't FIFO enough for crawling?
Answer: Need priority, recrawl deadlines, host politeness, and fairness.
Answer: URL dedupe prevents repeat URL work; content dedupe detects same/near-same page across URLs.
Answer: Safe concurrent serving, easy publication/rollback, background compaction.
Answer: Document sharding with replicated shards.
Answer: Parallel shard retrieval → local top-K → global merge/rerank.
Answer: Adaptive recrawl plus incremental fresh index segments.
Answer: Fan-out query latency is sensitive to the slowest shard.
Answer: Serving tombstones first, physical deletion later.
Answer: Frontier → fetch → parse/dedupe → index → shard retrieval → top-K merge/rank → results.

I would split web search into a crawl/index plane and a query-serving plane. A durable URL frontier prioritizes discovery and recrawls while enforcing per-host robots and politeness. Fetchers store raw pages; parsers normalize text, extract links, and perform URL/content deduplication. Incremental indexers build immutable compressed inverted-index segments, with document-sharded replicas for serving. At query time, the frontend parses and normalizes the query, fans it to one replica of each document shard, each shard uses postings and early termination to return local top-K, and an aggregator merges and reranks a small global candidate set before generating snippets. Adaptive recrawling and fresh index segments provide freshness; caching, hedged requests, and replicas control latency and availability.
Requirements, scale, freshness, and latency defined.
Canonicalization and URL seen checks covered.
Priority URL frontier and per-host politeness explained.
Robots, crawl budgets, traps, redirects, and conditional GET covered.
Raw storage, parsing, exact/near dedupe, and link graph covered.
Immutable incremental index construction and compaction covered.
Query parsing, parallel fan-out, local/global top-K, ranking, and snippets covered.
Caching, recrawl, deletion, autocomplete, spelling, and semantic extension covered.
Tail latency, failures, multi-region, security, and observability covered.
Detailed follow-ups, Q&A, and review quiz included.
Problem 22 | Geospatial Search, Map Tiles, Routing, Traffic, ETA & Location Updates

Design a Google Maps-style global mapping and navigation system. Users can browse maps, search places, request routes, receive turn-by-turn navigation, see live traffic, and share/update locations. The design must handle planetary-scale geospatial data, road graphs, enormous read traffic, frequent traffic updates, and low-latency routing.

Build a global maps platform that serves visual map data and place information, finds nearby places, computes routes over a massive road network, estimates travel time using current and historical traffic, and supports navigation as conditions change.
Why plain Dijkstra is insufficient at continental scale.
Location updates, privacy, and high-write telemetry.
Support driving first; walking/cycling/transit can be extensions.
Need map browsing, place search, nearby search, directions, and navigation.
Traffic should influence routes and ETA.
Map data changes much less frequently than traffic.
Need rerouting when user deviates or traffic changes materially.
Assume global coverage and hundreds of millions of users.
Street View and satellite imagery are optional follow-ups.

I’ll split the design into map rendering, place/geospatial search, routing, and dynamic traffic/navigation. Static map and road data are heavily preprocessed and versioned. The online routing service searches a partitioned road graph using hierarchical speedups, while a separate streaming traffic pipeline continuously updates edge travel-time weights. Clients cache tiles and navigation state so temporary backend/network failures do not immediately stop guidance.
Route from A to B with alternatives
Road closures, map corrections, new places
Transit, Street View, satellite, offline maps
place_id, name, categories, lat/lng, address, geometry, metadata
edge_id, from, to, distance, speed limit, restrictions, geometry
incoming edge, outgoing edge, rule/time window
route, destination, progress, current matched edge
anonymous/session/device context, lat/lng, speed, heading, time
Latitude/longitude identify positions on Earth but are awkward for direct rectangular indexing.
Use a projection such as Web Mercator for map tiles; routing still stores geographic coordinates/geometry.
Distance on Earth is not plain Euclidean over lat/lng for large distances.
Geohash/S2/H3-like hierarchical cells convert locations into spatial keys.
Hierarchical cells are useful for partitioning, nearby candidate discovery, aggregation, and traffic heatmaps.
Map tiling, geospatial place search, and road routing are related but different problems. A tile grid is not a routing graph, and a geohash alone is not a shortest-path algorithm.
Map tile pyramid across zoom levels
At zoom z, the world is divided into a 2^z by 2^z tile grid in common schemes.
Client requests only visible tiles plus a small prefetch margin.
Low zoom tiles contain generalized geometry; high zoom contains detailed roads/buildings/labels.
Tile URLs include map data/style version so they can be cached immutably.

18. Why Plain Dijkstra Is Not Enough

Router loads source/destination local partitions and high-level shortcuts.

Precompute and version the mostly static world—tiles, place indexes, road topology, and routing hierarchy—then continuously overlay dynamic traffic weights from privacy-controlled map-matched probes, allowing regional routing services to compute fast hierarchical shortest paths and clients to navigate reliably with cached route state.
Vector for dynamic styling; raster for imagery

Map data → versioned vector tiles/search index/road graph → CDN and regional services. Route request → snap to roads → hierarchical search with traffic-weighted edges → ETA/instructions. GPS probes → map matching → edge speed aggregation → live/predictive traffic weights → reroute only when useful.
Follow-up: Why can’t we just use Dijkstra for every route?

Detailed answer: Dijkstra gives the correct shortest path for nonnegative weights, but its search region can become enormous on a continental graph. A global road network contains tens or hundreds of millions of graph elements, and a route API must answer many requests concurrently. I would explain Dijkstra as the correctness baseline, then reduce search using A* and a hierarchical technique such as contraction hierarchies or multi-level partitioning. The route searches detailed streets only near the endpoints and uses precomputed high-level shortcuts for the long middle portion. This changes the online problem from exploring a large geographic area to exploring a much smaller relevant hierarchy.
Follow-up: How would you incorporate live traffic without rebuilding contraction hierarchies constantly?

Detailed answer: Separate topology preprocessing from dynamic weight customization. The road connectivity and shortcut structure change relatively slowly, while travel times change continuously. Precompute the hierarchy/shortcuts using topology and static attributes, then maintain shortcut weights derived from current edge weights. With customizable multi-level routing, traffic updates can recompute affected cell/boundary weights incrementally. If a particular hierarchy is difficult to update exactly, keep dynamic corrections at lower levels or use a hybrid A* around affected areas. The key is not rebuilding the entire graph for every speed sample.
Follow-up: How do you find nearby restaurants efficiently?

Detailed answer: Map the query location to a hierarchical spatial cell. Retrieve restaurant candidates from that cell and neighboring cells that cover the requested radius. The cell lookup is only a coarse filter: compute exact geographic distance for candidates afterward. Then apply category/open-now filters and rank by distance, text relevance, popularity, and quality. In dense areas, cells may be too large, so use finer cells or secondary partitioning. Continue expanding neighboring rings until enough candidates are collected or the radius is exhausted.
Follow-up: What is map matching and why is it necessary?

Detailed answer: Phone GPS is noisy and can place a car tens of meters away from its actual road, especially in cities, tunnels, or among tall buildings. Map matching converts a sequence of noisy coordinates into the most plausible road-edge sequence. For each point, generate nearby road candidates and score distance, heading, speed, and road type. Then use temporal continuity—often explained with an HMM/Viterbi-style model—to prefer a feasible sequence. Traffic aggregation and navigation progress should use matched edges rather than raw latitude/longitude.
Follow-up: How would you compute ETA for a one-hour trip?

Detailed answer: Do not sum every edge using the traffic speed observed at departure time. The user reaches later edges in the future. Starting from the departure timestamp, estimate the first edge travel time, advance the expected clock, then query the predicted travel time for the next edge at that future time. Continue along the route. Prediction can blend live speed, historical time-of-day/day-of-week patterns, recent trend, events, and weather. A final calibration model can correct systematic bias. This produces a time-dependent ETA.
Follow-up: How do you avoid rerouting the user constantly?

Detailed answer: Use hysteresis. A new route should replace the current route only when the user is confidently off-route, the current route becomes invalid, or the alternative provides a meaningful improvement beyond a threshold. Compare remaining ETA, reliability, tolls, and overlap. Require traffic changes to persist long enough to avoid reacting to noisy samples. Rate-limit reroutes and keep the current route if the difference is marginal. Otherwise navigation becomes unstable and frustrating.
Follow-up: How do map tiles scale?

Detailed answer: Pre-generate or incrementally generate versioned tiles for zoom levels. Store them in object storage and serve through a global CDN. The client requests only visible tiles plus a small prefetch ring and caches them locally. Because a tile URL contains the map/style version, published tiles are effectively immutable and can have long CDN TTLs. Vector tiles keep geometry compact and let the client style/render roads and labels; satellite imagery uses raster tiles.
Follow-up: How do you update one changed road without regenerating the world?

Detailed answer: Determine the affected geographic geometry. Rebuild only map tiles intersecting that geometry at relevant zoom levels, update the road-graph partition containing the edge and any impacted hierarchy boundary artifacts, and update search/geocoder data if addressability changed. Publish these artifacts under a new version. For an urgent closure, use the dynamic restriction layer immediately; the slower base-map rebuild can follow.
Follow-up: How do you model one-way streets and turn restrictions?

Detailed answer: Road edges are directed, so a one-way road simply has the permitted directed edge and not the prohibited reverse traversal. Turn restrictions are not captured by edge weights alone because legality can depend on the incoming edge. Model turn transitions explicitly or expand routing state to include the previous edge. Time-dependent restrictions—such as no turn during certain hours—are evaluated using traversal time.
Follow-up: How would you support transit?

Detailed answer: Transit is a different graph/time model. Stops and walking connections form nodes/edges, while trips follow schedules and service calendars. Use time-dependent routing algorithms and include transfers, walking, wait time, and real-time delay feeds. A multimodal route can connect walking → transit → walking. I would keep transit as a separate routing subsystem sharing place search, map rendering, and some navigation infrastructure.
Follow-up: How do you partition a global road graph?

Detailed answer: Use geographic cells/regions. Each partition owns internal road nodes/edges and identifies boundary nodes that connect to neighboring partitions. Hierarchical preprocessing computes intra-cell boundary shortcuts so long routes do not load every internal street. Dense cities can use smaller cells while rural areas use larger cells. Replicate boundary/neighbor metadata so route computation does not make excessive cross-service calls.
Follow-up: What if the traffic service is unavailable?

Detailed answer: Routing should not fail. Use the last known traffic snapshot if still reasonably fresh, then blend toward historical traffic profiles as data ages. If no dynamic data is available, route using historical/free-flow estimates. Mark internal confidence lower. Navigation remains functional, though ETA and congestion avoidance degrade. This is a good example of keeping dynamic traffic as an enhancement to a durable base road graph.
Follow-up: How do you detect traffic incidents from probes?

Detailed answer: Aggregate map-matched speeds by edge and short windows. Compare observed speed and volume against historical expectation and neighboring edges. A sharp persistent slowdown across connected edges can become an incident candidate. Combine this with explicit reports and provider feeds. Require confidence thresholds to prevent one faulty device from creating a false closure. Incident state should have lifecycle, severity, verification, and expiry.
Follow-up: How do you handle a GPS tunnel where location disappears?

Detailed answer: The client already has the route. It can estimate progress using last matched edge, speed/inertial signals if available, elapsed time, and route geometry. It should avoid aggressive rerouting while GPS confidence is low. When GPS returns, map-match the new point and reconcile progress. This is another reason navigation cannot depend on a server response for every location sample.
Follow-up: How would offline navigation work?

Detailed answer: Download a region package containing vector tiles, place/address subset, and compressed routing graph plus preprocessing artifacts. The device computes routes locally and caches maneuvers. Without network, live traffic, recent closures, and fresh POI data may be unavailable, so routing uses packaged/static or historical assumptions. When connectivity returns, apply delta updates and refresh dynamic restrictions.
Follow-up: What is the difference between geocoding and place search?

Detailed answer: Geocoding focuses on mapping an address or textual location representation to coordinates and vice versa. Place search is broader: businesses, landmarks, categories, aliases, popularity, and query intent. They can share indexes and entity IDs, but ranking and data sources differ. Nearby search additionally adds spatial radius/cell filtering.
Follow-up: How do you serve map data globally?

Detailed answer: Publish immutable map versions to object storage and CDN for tiles. Replicate place/geocoder indexes and road-graph partitions to regional serving clusters. Route users to nearby healthy regions. Dynamic traffic is streamed to the regions that need those edge weights. Because base artifacts are versioned, regions can roll forward independently and roll back safely.
Follow-up: How do you protect user location privacy while using it for traffic?

Detailed answer: Minimize collection and retention. For traffic, separate probe processing from account identity where possible, use short-lived identifiers, aggregate quickly to road-edge/window statistics, and discard raw precise points according to policy. Encrypt data, restrict access, and prevent aggregate outputs from exposing individual trajectories. Location sharing is a separate explicit user-facing authorization model.
Follow-up: How would you generate alternative routes?

Detailed answer: First compute the best path. To generate alternatives, use K-shortest/diverse-path techniques or temporarily penalize parts of the first route, then search again. Reject candidates that overlap too heavily or provide no meaningful choice. Rank the remaining few by ETA, reliability, tolls, distance, and user preferences. Do not return ten near-identical paths.
Follow-up: What is your failure strategy for navigation?

Detailed answer: The client stores the current route, maneuvers, geometry, and destination. If backend or network fails, it can continue guiding along that route. Tile cache keeps nearby map visible. If the user deviates while offline, local routing can help if an offline graph exists; otherwise guidance can resume after connectivity returns. Backend services are multi-region, and traffic/recommendation-like enhancements degrade before core route availability.
1. Why separate static road topology from dynamic traffic weights?

Detailed answer: Their update frequencies are radically different. Road connectivity changes comparatively slowly, while speeds can change every minute. Keeping topology versioned and stable lets us heavily preprocess routing structure and cache graph partitions. Traffic becomes a small dynamic overlay of edge costs and restrictions. This reduces rebuild cost and lets the routing service continue operating even when the traffic stream is delayed.
2. What is the role of a geospatial cell in routing?

Detailed answer: It is mainly an organizational and lookup primitive: partition the planet, find nearby objects, aggregate traffic, and identify road-graph partitions. It does not itself compute the shortest path. The routing algorithm runs over the road graph; cell boundaries and precomputed shortcuts help it skip large internal regions efficiently.
3. How would you snap a route endpoint to the road graph?

Detailed answer: Search nearby road segments using the spatial index. Score candidates by distance, heading if available, accessibility for the requested mode, and whether the point can legally enter the road. A point near a highway overpass must not automatically snap to the highway if the user is on the street below. Keep several candidates and let routing feasibility help disambiguate.
4. Why are vector tiles useful on mobile?

Detailed answer: They transmit compact geometry and semantic features instead of a fully rendered bitmap. The client can style labels, support dark mode/language changes, render crisply across pixel densities, and rotate/tilt the map. The trade-off is more client CPU/GPU work and rendering complexity. Satellite imagery remains raster because the source is photographic.
5. How do you avoid tile seams and inconsistent labels?

Detailed answer: Tile generation uses shared geometry boundaries and deterministic clipping/simplification. Labels are often placed with awareness beyond a single tile or the client performs cross-tile label collision resolution. Version all neighboring tiles consistently so a client does not combine incompatible map generations for long periods.
6. How would you store road geometry efficiently?

Detailed answer: Routing only needs compact topology and attributes in the hot path. Store node coordinates using delta/compressed representations and edge geometry as encoded polylines or references. Detailed geometry can be separated from the core graph and hydrated only for the final path. This keeps routing partitions memory-efficient.
7. How do time-dependent turn restrictions affect routing?

Detailed answer: The legality/cost of a transition may depend on the arrival time. The routing state therefore evaluates the restriction at the expected traversal timestamp. For example, a turn may be prohibited during rush hour. This makes the graph time-dependent; preprocessing must preserve correctness or route around dynamic restrictions in a lower-level search.
8. What happens if live traffic says a road is extremely fast because of bad data?

Detailed answer: Use validation and confidence. Reject impossible speeds, compare against speed limits and historical distributions, require multiple independent samples where possible, and cap how aggressively a single window can alter weight. Low-sample edges blend strongly with historical baseline. This prevents one faulty probe from producing unrealistic shortcuts.
9. How do you estimate traffic on roads with no probes?

Detailed answer: Use historical profiles, road class/speed limit, neighboring-edge conditions, time-of-day, and model-based inference. The system should attach lower confidence. Routing can still operate with free-flow or historical weights; coverage improves as probes arrive.
10. How would you scale map matching to millions of probes per second?

Detailed answer: Partition the stream by spatial cell or candidate road region. Keep compact road geometry/indexes in memory on workers. Process short sequences per device/session with bounded state, emit matched edge observations, and expire state quickly. Autoscale by stream lag. Hot urban cells can be split/salted while preserving enough sequence affinity for matching.
11. Why not store every user GPS point forever for better models?

Detailed answer: It is expensive and creates unnecessary privacy risk. Traffic primarily needs aggregated edge/time observations, and model training can often use privacy-preserving sampled/aggregated data. Retain raw precise trajectories only when there is a justified product need and policy basis, with strict retention and access controls.
12. How do you choose when to refresh a route due to traffic?

Detailed answer: Estimate the remaining ETA on the current route using the newest traffic and compare it with a newly computed best route. Reroute only if improvement exceeds a threshold or a closure invalidates the path. Threshold can depend on trip length: saving one minute on a one-hour trip may not justify disruption, while a major incident does.
13. How do you keep route instructions stable after small traffic updates?

Detailed answer: Instructions are tied to the chosen road-edge path, not continuously regenerated from every weight change. As long as the path remains valid and no reroute threshold is met, the client keeps the same maneuvers. ETA may update independently. This separates 'time estimate changed' from 'path changed'.
14. How do you calculate distance between two lat/lng points?

Detailed answer: For small local calculations, projected coordinates or a haversine/great-circle approximation are common. For nearby search, use spatial cells for coarse filtering and exact geographic distance for final candidates. Do not compare raw degree differences as if one degree had a constant physical length everywhere.
15. How do you handle countries with different map rules and data quality?

Detailed answer: Keep source provenance, region-specific validation, address formats, languages, road restrictions, and legal requirements in the map-data pipeline. Serving APIs expose a common entity/graph model, but ingestion and ranking can be locale-specific. Versioning lets regions update independently while preserving global interfaces.

Detailed answer: Street View is a separate imagery pipeline: capture panoramas, stitch/process them, geolocate along roads, blur sensitive content, store image pyramids, and serve through CDN. Map entities link road/place positions to panorama IDs. It shares geospatial indexing and CDN principles but is not part of the routing hot path.

Detailed answer: Ingest large georeferenced raster imagery, build multi-resolution tile pyramids, color-correct/stitch sources, and publish immutable raster tiles to CDN. Updates are batch-oriented and independent of road graph routing. The client overlays vector labels/roads when needed.
18. How do you prevent one dense city from overloading a routing shard?

Detailed answer: Replicate popular graph partitions across many routing workers and route requests using load-aware selection. Keep graph artifacts read-only/versioned so replication is cheap. For dynamic traffic, distribute compact weight updates to every replica. If a cell itself is too large, subdivide it while preserving hierarchy boundaries.
19. How do you roll out a new road graph safely?

Detailed answer: Build a complete new graph version and preprocessing artifacts offline. Validate connectivity, route regression tests, and sample ETAs. Load the version into a canary subset of routing workers, compare metrics, then increase traffic gradually. Keep the previous immutable version available for rollback. Never mutate the only live graph in place.
20. What is the final one-minute design summary?

Detailed answer: Static map data is ingested and published as immutable versions: vector/raster tiles for rendering, text+spatial indexes for places, and a partitioned directed road graph with hierarchical routing shortcuts. Tiles go through CDN. Route requests snap endpoints to roads and run a hierarchical A*/shortest-path search using live and predicted traffic weights. Traffic comes from privacy-controlled GPS/sensor streams, is map-matched to road edges, aggregated with confidence, and blended with historical patterns. Navigation clients cache route and maneuvers, send bounded progress updates, and reroute only for real deviation, closure, or meaningful ETA improvement. Regional replicas, versioned artifacts, dynamic closure overlays, and client-side fallback keep the system available.
A major stadium event ends and traffic changes in five minutes. What happens?

Probe volume rises around the stadium. Map-matching workers assign samples to outgoing road edges, and short-window aggregators detect speeds falling below historical expectations. Confidence rises quickly because many independent probes agree. Live weights propagate to routing replicas. New route requests avoid congested exits; existing sessions are reevaluated, but reroute hysteresis prevents unnecessary path changes. The predictive model also considers the event pattern for downstream edges.
A bridge closes suddenly. How do you remove it from routes immediately?

Create a dynamic closure restriction for the affected directed edges and publish it through a high-priority stream/cache invalidation path. Routing treats those edges as unavailable before the slower base-map update completes. Navigation sessions whose remaining path crosses the bridge are marked for reroute. Later, the map pipeline validates the closure and incorporates it into a new map/graph version if long-lived.
The user is on a parallel service road beside a highway. GPS is inaccurate. How do you avoid snapping incorrectly?

Generate both highway and service-road candidates. Distance alone is insufficient. Compare heading, speed, recent matched path, legal connectivity from the previous edge, and the sequence likelihood. The service road may be more consistent with previous points even if the highway is slightly closer geometrically. Maintain confidence and delay a hard switch until evidence is strong.
A region loses connectivity to the traffic stream. Can routing continue?

Yes. The routing graph and latest traffic snapshot are local. As live state ages, blend its influence down and rely more on historical traffic/free-flow. Route quality degrades gradually instead of failing. When the stream reconnects, apply newer edge versions/timestamps and discard stale updates.
A user requests a route from Delhi to Mumbai. Do we load every road in between?

No. The local detailed graph is searched near Delhi and Mumbai. The long middle portion uses a high-level highway/regional graph with precomputed shortcuts/boundary costs. Only partitions needed to expand the final route are hydrated for geometry and instructions. This is exactly why hierarchical routing is required.
Answer: To make published tiles immutable/cacheable and allow atomic rollout/rollback.
2. What is the baseline graph representation?
Answer: Directed road nodes/edges with distance, restrictions, and travel-time cost.
Answer: It explores too much of a massive graph per request.
Answer: Inferring the most likely road-edge sequence from noisy GPS observations.
5. How does live traffic reach routing?
Answer: Probe stream → map matching → window aggregation → edge weights → routing replicas.
Answer: Live probes are sparse/noisy and future route edges need prediction.
7. How do you avoid reroute flapping?
Answer: Hysteresis, confidence, thresholds, and rate limits.
8. What is the role of hierarchical spatial cells?
Answer: Partitioning, nearby candidate lookup, aggregation, and graph organization.
Answer: Dynamic restriction overlay before base-map rebuild.
Answer: Versioned static map artifacts + CDN/search/routing hierarchy, overlaid with streaming traffic and client-assisted navigation.

I would separate mostly static map data from highly dynamic traffic. The map pipeline publishes immutable vector/raster tiles, place/geocoder indexes, and a partitioned directed road graph with hierarchical routing shortcuts. Tiles are CDN-served. For directions, the service snaps endpoints to roads and uses hierarchical A*/shortest-path search rather than plain Dijkstra over the entire graph. GPS and sensor probes flow through map matching and windowed aggregation to produce live edge speeds, which are blended with historical/predicted traffic for routing and ETA. Navigation clients cache the route and maneuvers, progress locally, and request rerouting only on real deviation, closure, or meaningful time savings. Dynamic closure overlays, regional replicas, and offline/client fallback keep core navigation available.
