textRun.content: Design a Stock Exchange / Electronic Trading System
Problem 28 | Order Gateway, Matching Engine, Order Book, Sequencing, Market Data, Risk & Recovery

Design a low-latency electronic exchange that accepts buy/sell orders, enforces deterministic price-time priority, matches orders without double execution, publishes market data, survives failures without corrupting the order book, and provides a complete auditable event trail.
Why this is a new problem

Cloud file sync and ticket booking were already covered earlier, so this problem intentionally moves to a different architecture: deterministic single-writer matching, in-memory order books, write-ahead event logs, replay, market-data sequencing, and exchange-grade risk controls.
Cancel open order or modify according to exchange rules
Maintain bids and asks per instrument
Best bid/ask, depth, trades, sequence numbers
Extremely low and predictable latency on the critical path.
Deterministic matching: same ordered input must produce same output.
No double execution and no negative remaining quantity.
Strict ordering within each instrument/order-book ownership domain.
High availability without allowing two active matching owners for the same book.
Durable auditability of accepted orders, cancels and trades.
Market-data consumers must detect gaps and recover snapshots.
Performance isolation: analytics, reporting and persistence must not block matching.
We design an exchange matching venue, not a retail brokerage UI.
The exchange accepts orders from authenticated members/brokers.
Matching engine is the deepest component.
Clearing and settlement are downstream integrations, discussed but not implemented in full.
We prioritize limit-order-book trading; derivatives-specific margin is an extension.
One instrument is owned by exactly one active matching shard at a time.
client_order_id, account, instrument, side, type, price, qty, tif
An order's executed quantity + remaining quantity + cancelled/expired remainder must reconcile to the accepted quantity, subject to explicit replace semantics.
Member sends order over authenticated low-latency session.
Gateway validates protocol/session and assigns ingress metadata.
Pre-trade checks validate instrument, price bands, quantity and account limits.
Router sends instrument to its single active matching shard.
Ordered input is journaled/sequenced according to durability model.
Matching engine processes event against in-memory order book.
Engine emits order acknowledgement, fills/trades and book changes.
Execution reports return to involved members.
Highest price first; FIFO within same price
Lowest price first; FIFO within same price
Each price level maintains aggregate quantity and FIFO queue of orders.
Best bid is highest non-empty bid level; best ask is lowest non-empty ask level.
A buy limit order can match asks priced at or below its limit.
A sell limit order can match bids priced at or above its limit.
Remaining unmatched quantity rests on the book if time-in-force permits.
Better price wins first. At the same price, the earlier accepted order wins. This must be deterministic and based on exchange order, not client timestamps.
Match 100 @ $10.00 against first ask; incoming leaves 80.
Match 80 @ $10.05 against next ask; that ask leaves 70.
Incoming order is fully filled and does not rest.
Emit two trades and corresponding execution reports/book deltas in deterministic event order.
Find best price and insert/remove levels
For bounded tick ranges, array/ladder structures can outperform general trees. The interview point is O(1) or logarithmic best-price access plus fast cancel and FIFO at a price level.
13. Why Single Writer per Order Book
Concurrent mutation of the same book requires expensive locking and risks nondeterministic ordering.
One event loop owns the book and processes already ordered commands sequentially.
This makes price-time priority natural and simplifies replay.
Scale comes from many independent instruments/shards in parallel, not multiple writers to one book.
A very hot instrument can receive a dedicated core/process/machine.
Every accepted command in an ownership domain receives a monotonically increasing sequence.
New orders, cancels, replaces and administrative events participate in the same deterministic order.
Sequence is assigned before matching or at the matching owner as part of one ordered input stream.
Market-data and execution events reference input/output sequence positions.
Client timestamps are metadata, never authoritative matching order.
Journal accepted ordered commands or authoritative state transitions before considering them durable.
Replication strategy trades latency for failure tolerance.
Periodic snapshots capture in-memory book state at a known sequence.
Recovery loads latest snapshot and replays journal after that sequence.
Deterministic engine code must reproduce identical book/trade state from identical input.
Accepted order can vanish on crash
Machine loss may still lose unreplicated tail
There is no universal answer: exchanges choose a durability/latency contract. In an interview, state exactly what 'accepted' means and what failures can still lose an order.
Authenticate exchange member/session and enforce session-level sequence numbers.
Parse a compact binary protocol for predictable latency.
Reject malformed or duplicate session messages early.
Do not let gateway own order-book truth.
Throttle/rate-limit abusive or malfunctioning participants before they overload matching shards.
Put deterministic, necessary risk checks on the critical path; send heavier analytics and surveillance asynchronously. Cache reference/limit data close to the gateway/engine.
A market order consumes available opposite-side liquidity at best prices until filled or book is exhausted.
It has no protective limit unless the venue converts it to a market-with-protection rule.
Large market orders can walk multiple price levels.
Execution price can differ significantly from last traded price in a thin book.
Risk/price collars are important to prevent catastrophic erroneous orders.
Remain across sessions per venue rules
Execute entire quantity immediately or none
Must add liquidity; reject/cancel if it would cross
FOK may require checking executable quantity across eligible price levels before mutating the book, then executing atomically within the single-writer event.
Cancel identifies an open exchange order and removes remaining quantity if still active.
A cancel racing with a fill is resolved by sequencer order: whichever event reaches the engine first wins for the affected quantity.
Replace rules matter: increasing quantity or changing price commonly loses time priority.
A replace can be modeled as atomic cancel/new under exchange-specific semantics.
Execution reports tell the client whether cancel/replace succeeded or was too late.

Order O is resting. A marketable order and O's cancel arrive nearly simultaneously. Do not use locks/timestamps to guess. The sequencer establishes a total order for that book. If match command is first, the eligible quantity fills; if cancel is first, it is removed before matching.
Each match creates an immutable trade/execution identity.
Trade records include instrument, price, quantity, aggressor/resting order IDs and sequence/time metadata.
Order remaining quantities are updated in the same deterministic engine step.
Downstream clearing receives trade events asynchronously from authoritative log/output.
Corrections/busts are explicit later events, not silent mutation of historical trades.
Publish top-of-book, depth changes and trades independently from order-entry responses.
Every feed stream carries sequence numbers.
Gap recovery uses replay buffer or fresh snapshot plus subsequent deltas.
Slow consumers are never allowed to backpressure matching engines.
Consumer receives market-data deltas through sequence 50,000.
It detects next received message is 50,005.
If gap is too old/large, request book snapshot at sequence S.
Apply buffered deltas S+1 onward in order.
Resume live stream after sequence continuity is restored.
BBO contains highest bid and lowest ask plus quantities.
Depth feed contains multiple aggregated price levels.
Order-by-order feeds expose individual resting orders if venue provides them.
Market-data representation can be derived directly from matching-engine state changes.
Avoid querying the matching engine synchronously for every market-data consumer.
Best default; each book has one owner
Bad for matching because both sides meet on same book
Keep explicit directory so hot instruments can move/dedicate capacity.
All events for one instrument route to the same active owner.
Cross-instrument operations should not require synchronous global transactions on matching path.
Assign hot symbol to dedicated engine/core/process.
Avoid sharing CPU cache with many cold books.
Batch network I/O while preserving event order.
Use preallocated memory/object pools to reduce allocation/GC jitter.
Keep market-data fan-out outside the engine.
Capacity-plan for auction/open/close bursts, not only average QPS.
Pin matching thread to CPU core where infrastructure permits.
Keep book data in memory and cache-friendly structures.
Avoid blocking system calls on engine thread.
Avoid stop-the-world GC in latency-critical implementations; use appropriate language/runtime strategy.
Persist/replay asynchronously or through a carefully designed replicated journal path.

Do not run two independent active matching engines for the same instrument in different regions. They could both fill the same resting order. One active owner per book is the simplest correctness model.
Regions can be active for different instruments/shards.
Standby region continuously receives journal/state replication.
Failover promotes standby only after fencing the old owner.
Order gateways can be geographically distributed but forward to instrument home engine.
Market data can be replicated globally after authoritative matching.
Matching shard owner holds epoch/lease E.
All journal/state writes include epoch E.
Failure detector/control plane chooses replacement and increments epoch to E+1.
Storage/journal rejects stale writes from E.
Replacement loads latest snapshot and replays committed log.
Only after recovery does it accept new ordered commands.
Gateways refresh routing directory and send future orders to new owner.
Network requests can be duplicated; clients may retry after timeout.
Use session/client order IDs to deduplicate new-order commands.
Within the matching engine, each sequenced command is applied once to state.
Execution/trade IDs are stable and downstream consumers are idempotent.
The practical goal is exactly-once logical order acceptance/execution effects over replayable at-least-once transport.
Session protocol carries inbound/outbound sequence numbers.
On reconnect, member states last confirmed sequence.
Gateway replays missed execution/order reports from durable session/event history.
Duplicate client commands are rejected or mapped to existing order IDs.
Open-order snapshot can reconcile local client state.
Do not assume TCP continuity equals business-state continuity.
Instrument status is authoritative engine state: OPEN, HALTED, AUCTION, CLOSED, etc.
Status change is sequenced with order commands.
During halt, new/cancel behavior follows venue rules.
Resume/opening auction may use a different matching algorithm.
Market data publishes status transitions with sequence numbers.
Administrative controls need strong authorization and audit.
Collect orders during auction phase without continuous matching.
At uncross time, choose clearing price using venue-specific rules: maximize executable volume, minimize imbalance, tie-break appropriately.
Execute eligible orders deterministically at clearing price.
Transition remaining orders into continuous book per policy.
Auctions create extreme bursts and deserve separate capacity/testing.
Reject or constrain orders outside configured price collars.
Instrument-level volatility controls can pause trading after extreme moves.
Reference prices and band versions must be distributed consistently to risk/engine.
Control-plane updates are audited and sequenced into engine state when they affect matching eligibility.
A risk-control failure should fail safely according to venue policy.
Matching determines trades; clearing determines obligations between participants.
Trade capture stream sends immutable trade events downstream.
Clearing can net positions and calculate obligations outside matching latency path.
Settlement occurs later through securities/cash infrastructure.
A clearing outage should not silently mutate already executed exchange trades; buffer/replay downstream events.
Persist every accepted/rejected command and execution with participant/session/order identifiers.
Surveillance consumes events asynchronously for manipulation/abuse patterns.
Clock synchronization and precise timestamps support forensic analysis, but sequence is still the authoritative event order.
Audit logs should be append-only/tamper-evident according to regulatory requirements.
Operational debugging must reconstruct a book at any sequence.
Retry deduplicated by client/session order ID
Replay produces same fill/trade ID or authoritative output log prevents duplicate effect
Do not promote beyond known committed point without defined recovery
Matching continues; publisher rebuilds from event log/snapshot
Buffer immutable trade events; matching policy independent

Given snapshot at sequence 1,000,000 and commands 1,000,001..1,100,000, a recovered engine must produce the same final book and execution results as the original engine. Nondeterministic iteration order, wall-clock-dependent matching, random IDs, or concurrency inside one book can break this.
Generate trade IDs deterministically or persist authoritative outputs.
Use ordered data structures with defined traversal behavior.
Treat clock/time-based expiry as explicit sequenced events where needed.
Version matching rules so historical replay uses the correct logic.
Test replay hashes/checksums against production snapshots.
Putting the order book in a relational DB and locking rows for every match.
Using multiple active writers for one instrument.
Using timestamps instead of exchange sequence for priority.
Calling distributed transactions for every fill.
Letting market-data consumers query/block the matching engine.
Ignoring hot symbols and auction bursts.
Treating market data as reliable without sequence/gap recovery.
Failing over without fencing stale engine.
Putting analytics/surveillance on critical matching path.
Authenticated order gateways terminate participant sessions and perform cheap protocol checks.
Pre-trade risk validates instrument, price, size and participant limits close to the critical path.
Orders route by instrument to exactly one active matching owner.
A sequenced durable command journal defines deterministic input order.
The matching engine keeps the order book in memory and processes commands single-threaded per book/shard using price-time priority.
Executions and book deltas are emitted as ordered events.
Execution reports return to members while market data fans out independently with sequence numbers and snapshot/replay recovery.
Periodic snapshots plus replicated journal support deterministic failover.
Fencing epochs prevent two engines from owning the same book.
Clearing, surveillance, reporting and analytics consume immutable events asynchronously.

Shard by instrument, give each order book one fenced single-writer matching owner, sequence and durably journal commands, match entirely in memory with deterministic price-time priority, then publish executions and market-data deltas asynchronously while snapshots plus replay provide recovery.
Follow-up: Why not use a database transaction to match orders?

Detailed answer: The hot path needs deterministic microsecond-to-low-millisecond latency and operates on an ordered in-memory book. Row locks and distributed database coordination add jitter and contention. Durability comes from an ordered journal plus snapshots/replay, while the engine owns book mutation.
Follow-up: Why is a single writer not a scalability bottleneck?

Detailed answer: It is single writer per book or shard, not for the whole exchange. Thousands of instruments run in parallel across many engines. A hot instrument can receive dedicated hardware. Parallelizing mutation inside one book would complicate price-time ordering for limited benefit.
Follow-up: How do you implement price-time priority?

Detailed answer: Maintain bids by descending price and asks by ascending price. Each price level has FIFO orders in exchange-acceptance order. An incoming marketable order repeatedly consumes the best opposite level, then the oldest order at that price.
Follow-up: What if two orders arrive at exactly the same time?
Detailed answer: Physical simultaneity does not matter. The exchange sequencer establishes a deterministic order. Whichever command receives the earlier sequence has earlier time priority.
Follow-up: How do you handle cancel versus fill races?

Detailed answer: Both commands enter the same ordered stream for that book. If the incoming match event is sequenced first, eligible quantity fills before cancel. If cancel is first, the resting quantity is removed. The client gets a too-late cancel if it already filled.
Follow-up: Can an order be executed twice after failover?

Detailed answer: Logical effects must not duplicate. Inputs have stable IDs and ordered sequence. Recovery replays deterministically from a committed point, and trade IDs/output state are stable or persisted. Downstream consumers are idempotent.
Follow-up: When do you acknowledge a new order?

Detailed answer: After it has passed validation and reached the durability point promised by the venue. If the contract says accepted orders survive a machine loss, ACK must wait for the corresponding replicated durable commit, not just RAM.
Follow-up: How do you recover the order book?

Detailed answer: Load the latest snapshot taken at sequence S, then replay committed ordered commands S+1 onward. Because matching is deterministic, the resulting book should match the pre-failure state.
Follow-up: Why do you need fencing?

Detailed answer: Failure detection can be wrong during partitions. Without fencing, the old engine might continue matching while a new engine starts. Epoch tokens let the journal/state layer reject stale-owner writes so only the newest owner is authoritative.
Follow-up: How do you publish market data without slowing matching?

Detailed answer: The engine emits compact ordered book/trade events to a nonblocking output channel. Dedicated market-data services normalize and fan them out. Slow consumers are disconnected or recover from snapshot/replay; they never backpressure the engine.
Follow-up: How does a market-data client detect packet loss?
Detailed answer: Every feed stream has monotonic sequence numbers. A gap means loss. The consumer requests retained deltas or obtains a fresh snapshot at sequence S and then applies S+1 onward.
Detailed answer: By instrument/order book. All commands for one instrument route to one active shard. This preserves local ordering while different instruments match independently.
Follow-up: What about one extremely hot stock?

Detailed answer: Move it to a dedicated engine/core/machine, preallocate book memory, batch network I/O, isolate its market-data fan-out, and capacity-plan for opening/closing bursts. Do not split its price levels across independent writers unless using a much more complex specialized design.
Follow-up: How are partial fills represented?

Detailed answer: Each match emits an execution with fill quantity/price and decrements both orders' remaining quantity. The incoming order continues across levels until filled, no longer marketable, or constrained by time-in-force.
Follow-up: How do IOC and FOK differ?

Detailed answer: IOC executes immediately against available eligible liquidity and cancels any remainder. FOK requires the entire quantity to be immediately executable or executes nothing; the single writer can pre-check aggregate executable depth before mutation.
Follow-up: How does replace affect priority?

Detailed answer: Exchange rules define it. Commonly, price change or quantity increase loses time priority and behaves like cancel/new; quantity reduction at same price may retain priority. State the rule and implement it deterministically.
Follow-up: What happens if the market-data service is down?

Detailed answer: Matching and execution can continue if the venue's operating policy permits. Authoritative book events remain in logs. The market-data service restarts from snapshot/event replay. It is deliberately outside the matching critical path.
Follow-up: Why is wall-clock time not enough for audit order?

Detailed answer: Clock synchronization has error and concurrent systems can produce identical or skewed timestamps. Sequence number gives authoritative order; precise timestamps are supplemental forensic metadata.
Follow-up: How do you integrate clearing?

Detailed answer: Publish immutable trade-capture events after execution. Clearing consumes them idempotently and calculates obligations/netting outside the matching path. If clearing is unavailable, retain/replay the trade stream rather than blocking or rewriting matches.
Follow-up: Give the one-minute architecture summary.

Detailed answer: Members connect to low-latency order gateways. After protocol and pre-trade risk checks, each command routes by instrument to one fenced matching owner. Commands are sequenced and journaled according to the exchange's durability contract. The in-memory single-writer engine maintains bids/asks and applies deterministic price-time priority, producing stable executions and book deltas. Execution reports return to members; market-data services publish sequenced feeds independently with snapshot/gap recovery. Periodic snapshots plus replicated journals allow deterministic failover, while clearing, surveillance and analytics consume immutable events asynchronously.
1. Why is conversation-style distributed ordering not enough here?
Detailed answer: Trading needs deterministic price-time priority tied directly to mutable book state; the sequencing and single-writer engine are much tighter than ordinary messaging.
Detailed answer: Best ask minus best bid.
3. What does crossing the spread mean?
Detailed answer: A buy price is at/above best ask or sell price is at/below best bid, so it can execute immediately.
Detailed answer: Remaining unexecuted quantity of an order.
Detailed answer: The incoming order that removes resting liquidity.
Detailed answer: Fast cancellation/replacement without scanning price levels.
Detailed answer: Fast depth/BBO publication and executable-liquidity checks.
8. Can market data be eventually consistent?
Detailed answer: Consumers may receive asynchronously, but the feed itself must preserve detectable sequence order and recovery semantics.
Detailed answer: The exact input/output sequence through which snapshot state is complete.
Detailed answer: Lower parsing overhead, smaller messages and predictable latency.
Detailed answer: To reduce allocation/GC jitter on critical path.
Detailed answer: An authorized control preventing a participant/account/instrument from submitting eligible new orders.
Detailed answer: A configured acceptable price range used to reject/protect erroneous orders.
Detailed answer: Difference between executable buy and sell interest at candidate clearing prices.
Detailed answer: Historical replay must apply the rules that were active when events occurred.
16. What if a journal record is duplicated?
Detailed answer: Sequence/command IDs make replay idempotent; a committed sequence is applied once.
17. Can two symbols share one engine?
Detailed answer: Yes, if capacity permits; each remains logically ordered. Hot symbols can be isolated.
18. Why not partition a single book by user?
Detailed answer: Buyers and sellers must meet against one shared price-time priority state.
19. What is the key failover invariant?
Detailed answer: Never have two authoritative matching owners for the same instrument.
Detailed answer: The authoritative ordered command stream deterministically maps to one valid order-book and trade history.
An order is fully matched, but the engine crashes before the client receives the execution report.

The execution is already part of authoritative engine output/journal state. On recovery the engine does not create a new independent trade; deterministic replay or persisted output reconstructs the same trade ID. The member reconnects and replays missed execution reports.
A cancel and a market order hit the same resting order within microseconds.

Both are serialized by the book's sequencer. If cancel has the earlier sequence, the resting order is removed and cannot fill. If the market order is earlier, it fills eligible quantity and the later cancel may receive cancelled remainder or too-late status.
The primary engine is isolated from the control plane but still running.

The replacement can only become authoritative after a higher fencing epoch is established. Journal/state accepts writes only from the current epoch, preventing the isolated stale engine from committing new authoritative matches.

It detects a sequence gap. If replay retention covers the gap, fetch missing deltas and apply in order. Otherwise request a snapshot at sequence S, discard stale buffered events, apply deltas after S, and rejoin live feed.
A popular stock receives a huge opening-auction burst.

The instrument has dedicated capacity, preallocated memory and a specialized auction phase. Orders are collected without continuous matching; at uncross, the engine calculates the venue-defined clearing price and executes deterministically. Downstream market-data fan-out is isolated from matching.
If C is NEW BUY, inspect best ask.
While remaining_qty > 0 and best_ask <= buy_limit (or market order):
Take oldest resting order at best ask.
Remove filled resting order/empty price level.
If incoming remains and can rest, append to its bid price FIFO.

Keep the matching loop conceptually simple. The sophistication is in deterministic ordering, durability, recovery, hot-path isolation and failover, not in turning the algorithm into a distributed transaction.
No resting crossed book after event
The interview goal is not to invent nanosecond numbers. Show that every synchronous hop on the critical path is justified and everything else is moved downstream.
Answer: Highest price, then FIFO at that price.
Answer: Lowest price, then FIFO at that price.
Answer: Deterministic mutation and price-time ordering without locks.
Answer: At the explicitly defined durable commitment point.
Answer: Snapshot plus deterministic journal replay.
Answer: Sequence gap -> replay or snapshot + deltas.
Answer: Shard by instrument; isolate hot symbols.
9. How do you prevent split brain?
10. What stays off the critical path?
Answer: Market-data fan-out, analytics, surveillance, reporting and most downstream clearing work.

I would shard the exchange by instrument and give each order book exactly one fenced active matching owner. Order gateways authenticate members and run pre-trade checks, then commands are sequenced and durably journaled according to the venue's acceptance contract. The matching engine keeps bids and asks in memory and processes one ordered event stream using deterministic price-time priority, including partial fills, cancels and replaces. It emits immutable trades, execution reports and book deltas. Market data is published independently with sequence numbers and snapshot/gap recovery. Periodic snapshots plus journal replay recover an engine, while fencing prevents split-brain ownership. Clearing, surveillance and analytics consume the authoritative event stream asynchronously.
Functional requirements and explicit acceptance semantics.
Order state machine and idempotent client order IDs.
Market orders, IOC/FOK and replace semantics.
Sharding by instrument and hot-symbol isolation.
Trading halts, auctions and circuit breakers.
20 detailed follow-ups, 20 additional Q&As, 5 scenarios, invariants, latency drill and colorful diagrams.
54. Deep Dive: Order Book Memory Layout and Complexity
Ordered tree/skip structure or bounded price ladder
O(1) to O(log P) depending representation
O(log P), or O(1) in indexed ladder
O(1) average lookup plus level cleanup

The number of individual fills is unavoidable work: an incoming order that consumes 10,000 resting orders must create 10,000 logical executions. The optimization target is eliminating unrelated scans, allocations, locks, database calls and network waits from that loop.
Use stable order nodes so the cancellation hash map points directly to the order's queue position.
When the last order leaves a price level, remove that level and advance the best-price pointer.
Keep aggregate level quantity updated in the same single-writer transition as individual order quantities.
Represent monetary prices as integer ticks/fixed-point values, not binary floating point.
Pre-size common structures and use object pools/arenas where latency jitter matters.
Book snapshots should serialize enough priority information to reconstruct FIFO order exactly.
55. Deep Dive: Replace, Priority and Self-Trade Prevention
Replace semantics are an interviewer favorite because a careless implementation can let a participant jump the queue. The exchange must define which modifications preserve priority.
Immediate if cancel event wins sequence

Self-trade prevention (STP) is another venue rule. If two orders from the same participant/account would trade, configured policy may cancel the aggressor, cancel the resting order, decrement both without a trade, or allow the trade. The policy must be deterministic and evaluated inside the matching event before an execution is emitted.
STP identifiers must be validated before the order reaches the book.
STP actions are auditable events and must preserve sequence ordering.
Do not implement STP as a delayed downstream cleanup; once a trade is published, reversing it is materially different.
Replace and STP rules must be versioned so deterministic historical replay uses the correct policy.
56. Deep Dive: Failure Timeline - Primary Matching Engine Crash
At sequence 9,000,000 the engine has a snapshot persisted at sequence 8,950,000.
Commands through 9,000,000 are committed in the authoritative replicated journal.
The primary process crashes before some clients receive their latest execution reports.
Control plane establishes a new ownership epoch and fences the failed/stale owner.
Standby loads snapshot 8,950,000 and replays 8,950,001 through 9,000,000.
Replay regenerates or verifies the same deterministic order state and execution identities.
Gateway routing is switched to the recovered owner only after it reaches the committed frontier.
Client sessions reconnect and replay missed ACK/execution reports from their last confirmed outbound sequence.
New commands are then accepted under the new ownership epoch.

The critical distinction is committed versus merely observed work. A response that reached a client must correspond to an authoritative committed state under the exchange's acceptance contract. Conversely, an uncommitted speculative command must not suddenly appear as a valid order after failover.
57. Deep Dive: Disaster Recovery and Regional Strategy
Keep matching authority local to one region/site per instrument to avoid WAN consensus on every book mutation.
Replicate journals and periodic snapshots to a secondary failure domain according to the recovery-point objective.
Warm standby processes can continuously validate replay and maintain near-current in-memory state without becoming authoritative.
Promotion requires explicit fencing and routing-directory update; DNS alone is too weak for ownership correctness.

Define whether a full-site disaster can lose the last unreplicated microseconds of accepted work. If the answer is no, remote synchronous durability belongs on the critical path and increases latency.
Run scheduled disaster-recovery exercises that compare recovered book hashes, open orders, executions and market-data sequence frontiers.
Market-data recovery can be slower than matching-state recovery, but consumers need a new snapshot/sequence epoch if feed continuity changes.
Follow-up: Why use integer ticks instead of floating point prices?

Detailed answer: Binary floating point can represent decimal prices imprecisely. Convert valid prices to integer tick units or fixed-point representation so comparisons and equality are deterministic.
Follow-up: How would you support stop orders?

Detailed answer: Keep inactive conditional orders outside the visible executable book. When the venue-defined trigger condition occurs, create a sequenced activation event that converts the stop into its resulting order type. Trigger rules and activation ordering must be explicit.
Follow-up: How do you prevent a stale gateway from routing to an old engine?

Detailed answer: Gateways cache a versioned routing directory but engine/journal fencing is the final protection. Even if a stale gateway sends to the former owner, that owner cannot commit authoritative commands under the old epoch.
Follow-up: Can snapshots be taken without stopping trading?

Detailed answer: Yes. The single-writer can mark an exact sequence boundary and copy/serialize state using a coordinated snapshot technique or hand immutable/copy-on-write state to a snapshot worker. The snapshot must correspond to one unambiguous sequence.
Follow-up: What happens when an order references an unknown cancel target?
Detailed answer: Return a deterministic cancel reject/unknown-order response. Never create state merely to satisfy a cancel.
Follow-up: How do you reconcile clearing with the exchange after an outage?

Detailed answer: Replay trade-capture events by stable trade sequence/ID. Clearing acknowledges its consumed frontier; duplicates are ignored idempotently. Compare trade counts/quantities and sequence ranges rather than relying on best-effort delivery.
Follow-up: How do you test a matching engine?

Detailed answer: Use property tests for invariants, deterministic replay tests, model-based comparison against a simple reference matcher, randomized cancel/replace races, crash-at-every-sequence tests, auction tests and high-volume latency benchmarks.
Follow-up: What data should be in an order-book snapshot?

Detailed answer: Instrument status, all live orders with IDs/side/price/remaining quantity and exact FIFO priority, relevant sequence/epoch, and any matching-rule state needed to continue deterministically.
Follow-up: What is the danger of asynchronous risk state?

Detailed answer: If two gateways independently consume the same remaining credit without coordination, aggregate exposure can exceed limits. Use partitioned account risk ownership, reserved limits, or a clearly defined conservative distributed limit mechanism.
Follow-up: How would you support multiple asset classes?

Detailed answer: Keep a common ordered gateway/journal framework but allow instrument-specific matching/risk rule modules. Equities, options and futures can differ in tick sizes, auctions, margin and session rules; version those rules explicitly.
Draw client/member -> gateway -> risk -> instrument router -> sequencer/journal -> matching engine.
Inside the engine draw bids on the left, asks on the right, FIFO queues at each price.
Show executions returning to members and book/trade events leaving through a separate market-data publisher.
Below the engine draw snapshot + replicated journal + standby replay.
Add a routing directory/fencing epoch to explain failover.
Finally add clearing/surveillance asynchronously so the interviewer sees they do not block matching.

textRun.content: Design Google Docs / Real-Time Collaborative Editor
Problem 29 | Realtime Collaboration, OT/CRDT, Presence, Versioning, Offline Editing & Conflict Resolution

Design a collaborative document editor where many users can edit the same document concurrently, see changes with low latency, reconnect safely, work offline, preserve a durable revision history, and converge to the same document despite reordering, retries and failures.

The difficult part is not storing text. It is defining how concurrent edits are ordered or merged so every replica converges without losing user intent. Separate the realtime collaboration stream from durable snapshots, revision history, permissions, search and exports.
Edit rich text: insert/delete characters, paragraphs and formatting.
Multiple users edit the same document concurrently.
Show collaborator cursors, selections and presence.
Offline editing followed by safe synchronization.
Low perceived edit latency, typically local-first rendering.
All connected replicas eventually converge to identical document state.
Support millions of documents and many active collaboration sessions.
Reconnect and duplicate delivery must be safe.
Durable history must survive collaboration-server failure.
Presence/cursor traffic must not overload durable storage.
Strong global consistency across unrelated documents is unnecessary.
Within one collaboration session, edits use a well-defined revision/order or convergent CRDT model.
Local keystrokes appear immediately before server round trip.
Server acknowledgement means the operation is durably represented in the authoritative history.
Permissions are strongly checked when joining and periodically revalidated.

55. Deep Dive: Comments, Suggestions, and Stable Anchoring

A comment should not be anchored only by numeric character offsets because concurrent inserts and deletes shift those offsets. Anchor it to logical document positions or node/range identifiers that participate in the same transformation/merge model as edits.

When a range is partially deleted, shrink the comment anchor to the surviving content. When the entire range disappears, retain an orphaned/collapsed anchor according to product policy so the discussion is not silently lost.

Suggestion mode is not merely colored text. A suggested insertion/deletion has author, creation revision, state, and a target range. Accepting or rejecting it generates canonical document operations so every collaborator observes the same result.
Comments can have their own versioned thread state—open, resolved, reopened—without forcing every comment message into the character-edit operation stream.
Mention notifications are asynchronous. First commit the comment/suggestion, then emit a notification event; a notification outage must not roll back the document.
56. Deep Dive: Document Schema and Structural Editing
Real editors contain paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, code blocks, links, footnotes, images and formatting spans. Model the document as a validated tree rather than one giant string.

Structural operations include split paragraph, join blocks, wrap list, insert table row, delete node, move node and apply mark. Each operation defines valid preconditions and deterministic behavior under concurrency.
Node identifiers reduce ambiguity when a remote operation refers to content whose surrounding character positions changed.
Schema validation runs before commit so malformed client operations cannot corrupt the shared document tree.
Schema migrations are versioned. A recovered historical operation must be interpreted under compatible rules, or snapshots must be migrated before replay.
Large pasted content should be chunked/batched into bounded operations so one client cannot monopolize the collaboration event loop.
57. Deep Dive: Testing the Collaboration Algorithm
Property test convergence: generate concurrent operation sets, deliver them in allowed different orders, and verify all replicas end with the same document.
Property test preservation: characters inserted by a user should not disappear unless a causally valid delete removes them.
Run randomized insert/delete/format workloads against a simple reference implementation.
Crash the leader at every point around append, ACK and broadcast; retries must never duplicate a logical operation.
Simulate offline clients that reconnect after thousands of revisions and after compaction boundaries.
Inject duplicate, delayed and reordered network frames; op_id/revision handling must remain correct.
Compare document checksums at canonical revision boundaries and alert on divergence.
Load-test viral documents separately from the normal many-small-documents workload.
Follow-up: Can the collaboration server keep the whole document only in memory?
Detailed answer: It can cache the hot document in memory, but durable operation history and snapshots remain authoritative. A process crash must be recoverable without relying on its RAM.
Follow-up: What happens if a remote operation arrives before an earlier revision?
Detailed answer: Do not apply it blindly. Buffer until the missing revision arrives or trigger gap recovery. Canonical revision continuity is part of the client protocol.
Follow-up: How do you move a comment when text before it is inserted?
Detailed answer: Transform its anchor positions using the same positional semantics as document operations, or use stable logical anchors whose relative positions survive the insert.
Follow-up: How do you prevent one paste from blocking everyone?
Detailed answer: Set operation-size limits, chunk large structural changes, bound per-event work, and yield/batch fan-out while preserving canonical ordering.
Follow-up: What if the same user edits from two devices offline?

Detailed answer: Treat devices as independent replicas with stable operation identities. On reconnect, both sets merge against server state using the chosen OT/CRDT semantics; user identity alone must not imply one linear local history.
Follow-up: Can the server broadcast before durable append?
Detailed answer: It can reduce latency speculatively, but then clients may observe edits that disappear after failure. A simpler interview contract is durable commit before canonical ACK/broadcast.
Follow-up: How do you know a snapshot is safe to use?
Detailed answer: It carries doc_id, exact canonical revision, schema version and checksum. Recovery replays only operations after that revision and can verify resulting checksum/invariants.
Follow-up: What if the operation log is temporarily unavailable?
Detailed answer: Stop acknowledging new canonical edits or enter an explicitly defined degraded mode. Do not claim edits are saved if the durability contract cannot be met.
Follow-up: How do you support read-only public documents cheaply?
Detailed answer: Serve a recent immutable/materialized snapshot from CDN/read replicas and optionally stream public deltas; do not allocate full editor session state to every viewer.
Follow-up: What is the hardest correctness bug?

Detailed answer: Replica divergence: two users believe they are at the same revision but render different state. Detect it with revision/checksum telemetry and recover via authoritative snapshot resync.
